Audit Analytics with CaatMaster

A practitioner’s guide to testing for error, omission, and fraud, using computer-assisted audit techniques, financial statement analytics, and AI-assisted review.

Parts I–VIII: Complete 32 Chapters Companion to CaatMaster

Part I

Foundations

Chapter 1

What This Book Is About

Financial statements can be wrong for reasons that have nothing to do with dishonesty. A clerk enters an invoice twice because two people happened to process the same batch of mail on the same afternoon. A finance team continues to apply a depreciation rate that was correct for one class of equipment to a newly acquired class that depreciates differently. A revenue recognition policy that was appropriate under a prior accounting standard is left unchanged after the standard was replaced. None of these situations involves an intention to deceive, and each of them can materially misstate a set of financial statements.

Fraud does happen, and this book addresses it directly, in the chapters on segregation of duties, Benford’s Law, and journal entry testing, among others. But an audit methodology built primarily around catching dishonest people misses most of what actually goes wrong in financial reporting. In most engagements, the majority of findings trace back to error, to control weaknesses that permit error to go undetected, and to the misapplication of judgment on accounting estimates that are inherently difficult to get exactly right. A well designed set of audit analytics has to surface all three causes, and it has to do so without prejudging which one it has found.

This distinction is central enough to the way this book is written that it recurs as a deliberate discipline in every technique chapter. Each chapter that introduces an analytical method closes with a section titled Interpreting the Result, and that section asks the same three questions in the same order every time: what benign, procedural explanation would produce this pattern; what error or lapse in judgment would produce it; and what would have to be true for the pattern to reflect deliberate manipulation. A flagged transaction is the beginning of an inquiry, not the end of one. A reader who works through the technique chapters while skipping this framing will still learn to operate CaatMaster competently. That reader will not learn to use it the way an experienced audit senior does, which is to treat every exception as a question addressed to a specific person, most of whom can answer it in a single sentence.

What CaatMaster Is

CaatMaster is a desktop application for computer-assisted audit techniques, built for auditors, internal control specialists, and compliance officers who need to examine a complete population of transactions rather than a sample of them. It combines three kinds of capability that are usually found in separate tools: general-purpose data transformation and cleaning, of the kind found in a spreadsheet or a business intelligence product; a library of audit-specific analytical tests, ranging from long-established techniques such as Benford’s Law and gap analysis to statistical estimates required by specific accounting standards such as IFRS 9 and IAS 36; and a set of AI-assisted features for working with narrative text and unstructured documents, designed under a strict rule described in Chapter 4 that the AI is never asked to count, sum, or estimate a figure that Polars, the underlying data engine, can compute exactly.

Every operation applied to a dataset in CaatMaster is recorded as a named, ordered step. This record, called the Applied Steps pipeline, can be reviewed, reordered, disabled, or reapplied to a refreshed extract of the same data without repeating the analysis by hand. The purpose of this design is reproducibility. An audit finding that cannot be regenerated from the same inputs by a different reviewer is a weak finding, regardless of how interesting it looked the first time it appeared. Chapter 2 describes this pipeline and the rest of the application’s structure in detail.

Who Should Read This Book

This book is written for three overlapping audiences. External and internal auditors will use it as a guide to running substantive tests and control evaluations inside CaatMaster, and as a reference for the accounting and statistical reasoning behind each test, not only the sequence of buttons that runs it. Risk and compliance officers will use it to design recurring, self-administered reviews ahead of a formal audit. Engagement leaders and audit methodology staff will use the later chapters, particularly those on audit programs and reporting, to standardize procedures across a team so that the same test performed by two different people produces the same result.

The book assumes a working knowledge of financial statements and of the audit process generally. It does not assume prior experience with a specific CAAT tool, with Python, or with statistics beyond what a professional accounting qualification already covers. Where a technique depends on a statistical concept that a reader might not have encountered, such as the interquartile range or a z-score, that concept is explained at the point where it is first used rather than gathered into a separate mathematics appendix.

How This Book Is Organized

The eight parts of this book move from general capability toward specific application. Part I, which this chapter opens, covers the application itself: its structure, how to bring data into it without corrupting the very numbers under examination, and the design philosophy that separates deterministic calculation from AI assistance. Part II covers the classic techniques common to almost every CAAT tool: profiling, completeness testing, cross-tabulation, Benford’s Law, ratio analysis, anomaly detection, and sampling. Part III addresses internal control testing under the frameworks most commonly referenced in a financial statement audit, the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and the COSO Internal Control Framework. Part IV takes up the estimate-heavy areas of International Financial Reporting Standards where a recalculation, rather than a simple exception test, is the appropriate audit response: revenue recognition, expected credit losses, leases, impairment, provisions, inventory, tax, and foreign currency.

Part V returns to a problem introduced in Chapter 3 and treats it at full length: getting genuinely reliable figures out of a client’s own reporting, whether that reporting arrives as a spreadsheet or as a structured XBRL filing. Part VI covers the AI-assisted features in detail, beginning with the architectural pattern that keeps them from inventing figures. Part VII covers what happens after an analysis is complete: visualizing results, building a report, saving a procedure for reuse next year, and managing the underlying projects and datasets. Part VIII closes the book with two chapters on the limits of everything that came before it, on professional skepticism as an operating discipline rather than a slogan, and on the data governance obligations that a tool like this one creates for the firm that deploys it.

How to Read This Book

Readers who are new to computer-assisted audit techniques generally are encouraged to read Parts I and II in sequence before working on a live engagement, since later chapters assume familiarity with the Applied Steps pipeline and with the general shape of a CaatMaster analysis. Readers who already have experience with a CAAT tool such as ACL or IDEA may move directly to Part III or Part IV and treat Parts I and II as a reference, consulted when a specific mechanism, such as the numeric parsing behavior covered in Chapter 3, needs clarification.

Every technique chapter in Parts II through V follows the same internal structure: an explanation of what the technique detects and why it matters, instructions for running it inside CaatMaster, an explanation of the calculation performed underneath the interface, a worked case study with realistic figures, and an Interpreting the Result section that applies the three-question discipline described earlier in this chapter. A reader in a hurry before a specific procedure can go directly to the how-to-run-it section of the relevant chapter. A reader building genuine competence in audit analytics, rather than familiarity with one tool’s menus, should read the surrounding sections as well, since the underlying reasoning is what continues to apply after the software changes.

A note on terminology

Throughout this book, the word finding refers to any pattern surfaced by an analytical procedure, without regard to its eventual cause. The word exception is used interchangeably with finding. Neither word implies fraud, error, or wrongdoing of any kind. Where a specific cause is meant, this book says so directly.

Chapter 2

Getting to Know CaatMaster

A CAAT tool is judged, in practice, less by the sophistication of any single test it offers than by how easily an auditor can trust the trail leading to that test’s result. This chapter describes the structural features of CaatMaster that exist to support that trust: the project and dataset model, the Applied Steps pipeline, and the arrangement of views that an auditor moves between during a typical engagement.

Projects and Datasets

Work in CaatMaster is organized into projects. A project corresponds, in most cases, to a single audit engagement or a single recurring compliance review, and it holds every dataset, transformation, and saved analysis associated with that engagement in one file. A dataset is a single table of data brought into the project, whether that table originated as a comma-separated export from a general ledger system, a worksheet from an Excel workbook, or the output of a query against a client’s database.

A project can hold any number of datasets, and datasets within a project can be joined, appended, or compared against one another. This matters for tests that depend on more than one source at once. A three-way match between a purchase order, a goods received note, and an invoice, for example, requires three separate datasets to be joined on a common key before the comparison can run; Chapter 6 works through this exact procedure. Because the join itself is recorded as a step, the three-way match can be rerun automatically the following quarter against refreshed extracts of the same three tables.

The Applied Steps Pipeline

Every transformation applied to a dataset, from a simple column rename to a statistical calculation with a dozen parameters, is recorded as a step in that dataset’s Applied Steps pipeline. The pipeline is visible at all times as an ordered list alongside the data itself. A step can be temporarily disabled without being deleted, which allows an auditor to compare a dataset’s state before and after a given transformation without losing either version. A step can also be reordered, subject to the transformations later in the pipeline still being valid against the changed sequence, and the entire pipeline can be reapplied in one operation to a freshly imported version of the same source file.

This last capability is what makes a procedure genuinely reusable rather than merely repeatable by manual reconstruction. An audit program built once, during the current year’s engagement, against this year’s trial balance extract can be saved and, in the following year, pointed at next year’s extract with the same column names, producing the same tests without the auditor rebuilding a single step. Chapter 29 covers the mechanics of saving and reusing an audit program in this way.

Why this matters for review

A second reviewer examining a finding does not need to take the first preparer’s word for how a number was produced. The Applied Steps pipeline for the dataset that produced it is a literal, ordered record of every transformation involved, from the original import to the final flag. This is the same principle that underlies a well-documented spreadsheet formula, applied at the level of an entire analysis rather than a single cell.

Moving Around the Application

CaatMaster presents its functionality through a set of views, reached from the sidebar, each responsible for one stage of the work. The Data view displays the current state of a dataset in a table and is where a dataset is first imported. The Transform view exposes the Applied Steps pipeline described above and is where the great majority of the transformations and tests covered in this book are actually run, since every statistical, audit, financial, and machine-learning operation opens as a dialog on top of it, in one of the three ways described below. The SQL Query view provides a direct SQL interface against every dataset currently open in the project, useful when a question is more naturally expressed as a join or an aggregation than as a sequence of individual operations. The Visualizations view builds charts from any dataset in the project. The Reports view assembles findings into a document for distribution, covered in Chapter 28. The Projects view manages the engagements themselves, and the Dashboard view gives a summary of recent activity across the current project.

A single dataset can be worked on from more than one view without conflict, because every view operates against the same underlying Applied Steps pipeline for that dataset. A transformation applied from the Transform view is immediately reflected in the Data view’s table, and a chart built in the Visualizations view against a dataset updates automatically if an upstream step in that dataset’s pipeline is later modified.

Three Ways to Reach an Operation

Every technique chapter in this book states, precisely, where the operation it covers is found, because CaatMaster genuinely offers three different starting points, and they are not interchangeable. Getting this distinction wrong is the single most common way an instruction in a CAAT tool’s documentation fails to match what a reader sees on their own screen, so it is worth establishing clearly here rather than leaving it to be inferred chapter by chapter.

The first path is the sidebar itself. A small number of features, Profile Dataset, Verify Data, Variables Sampling, and Audit Programs under the Analyze heading, along with Join Datasets, Append Datasets, Compare Datasets, and Fuzzy Match Datasets under Combine, are reached only from the sidebar. Most of these are standalone tools rather than steps in the Applied Steps pipeline; Profile Dataset and Verify Data, for instance, produce a read-only report and never modify the underlying dataset.

The second path is the top menu bar: File, Transform, Audit, Statistics, Reports, AI, ML, and View. Each of these menus holds a curated, thematically grouped subset of the full operation catalog, promoted to a permanent, one-click location because it is used frequently enough to deserve one. The Audit menu’s Audit Checks submenu, for example, includes Benford’s Law Analysis, Outlier Detection, and Round Number Analysis, all covered in this book, but does not include every audit-related operation CaatMaster offers.

The third path is the one that actually reaches everything: right-clicking any column header in the Transform view’s data grid. This opens a menu of quick, one-click actions for that specific column, Sort Ascending, Sort Descending, Remove, and Visualize, followed by a complete, category-organized listing of every single operation in the application, including a number of Statistics and Machine Learning operations, such as Quick Stats and Group Summary, that have no shortcut anywhere in the top menu bar or the sidebar. A reviewer who cannot find an operation in either of the first two locations should always try this third path before concluding the feature does not exist. Appendix A lists every operation this menu contains, organized by the same categories the menu itself uses, together with where else, if anywhere, each one can also be reached.

Working Across Multiple Datasets

Several of the techniques in this book, including the three-way match mentioned earlier and the segregation of duties analysis in Chapter 12, depend on bringing together data that arrives as separate extracts: a purchase order table, a goods received table, an invoice table, a user access log. CaatMaster handles this through the Join Datasets and Append Datasets operations, both of which are recorded as ordinary steps in the resulting dataset’s pipeline in the same way as any single-table transformation.

A join produces a new dataset combining columns from two existing ones, matched on a key that need not share the same name in both source tables. An append stacks two datasets with compatible columns into one, useful for combining several months of transaction extracts into a single population before running a test across the full period. Both operations are ordinary, replayable steps, which means a monthly append-and-test procedure, once built, runs identically every month without being rebuilt from source files each time.

Chapter 3

Getting Your Data In Correctly

No analytical technique in this book can produce a correct result from a number that was misread on the way into the application. This sounds obvious enough to skip past, and it is skipped past often enough in practice that misread figures are among the most common causes of a wrong audit conclusion produced by software rather than by a person. This chapter covers the specific ways a financial figure can be misread during import, and the features CaatMaster provides to prevent it.

The Problem with Ordinary Numbers

A number as it appears in an accounting export rarely looks like a number as a computer understands one. A trial balance extracted from an enterprise resource planning system typically presents amounts with a thousands separator, so that one million two hundred thirty-four thousand five hundred sixty-seven dollars appears as 1,234,567 rather than 1234567. A negative amount, following long-standing accounting convention, is frequently shown in parentheses rather than with a leading minus sign, so that a credit balance of eight hundred thousand dollars appears as (800,000). A figure copied from a report generator may carry a currency symbol, a percent sign, or trailing whitespace.

A general-purpose data tool that reads a column of such values without accounting for these conventions has two possible failure modes, and both are worse than an outright error message. The first is that the import fails to recognize the column as numeric at all, and every subsequent calculation against it silently returns nothing, without necessarily producing a visible error if the calling code tolerates missing values. The second, more dangerous failure, is that the import partially succeeds: some rows in the column parse correctly and others silently become null, so that a sum, an average, or a ratio computed from the column is quietly built from an incomplete population, with no indication in the resulting figure that anything was dropped.

A scenario worth recognizing

Suppose an internal audit team imports a subsidiary’s trial balance into a general-purpose analytics tool ahead of a quarterly review. The Amount column, as exported from the subsidiary’s accounting system, uses a thousands separator throughout and represents every credit balance in parentheses. The import tool recognizes the column as text, since none of its values match a bare numeric pattern, and the team’s workflow calls for casting the column to a number before running any ratio tests. The cast succeeds for values without a comma, such as small expense line items, and fails silently for every larger balance, which is to say for nearly every asset and liability account that matters. The resulting current ratio, computed from a current assets total that is missing most of its constituent accounts, comes out below one, and the team could spend a full day investigating an apparent liquidity problem that does not exist before tracing the discrepancy back to the import step.

A reader whose own import process casts a text column to a number in a single step, without a validated intermediate parse, is exposed to exactly this failure mode, whether or not it has yet produced a wrong ratio that anyone noticed.

How CaatMaster Parses a Number

CaatMaster resolves a value formatted this way by recognizing, rather than merely stripping, the specific conventions that a financial figure uses. A recognized currency symbol or a small set of common ISO currency codes at the start of the value is removed. A parenthesized value, with or without a preceding currency symbol, is treated as negative and its sign is applied after the surrounding punctuation is removed. A trailing minus sign, occasionally produced by older accounting systems, is moved to the front of the value before parsing. Thousands separators are removed once the value has been confirmed, by pattern, to actually be a number rather than a piece of text that happens to contain digits.

That last qualification matters as much as the parsing rules themselves. A parser that strips every character that is not a digit, a decimal point, or a minus sign will, in the course of correctly handling 1,234,567, also convert a quarter label such as Q1 into the number one, and a fiscal year reference such as FY2023 into the number two thousand twenty-three. Both of these are real values that appear routinely in period columns and reference numbers throughout a financial dataset, and misreading either one as a numeric account balance would be a worse outcome than failing to parse it at all. CaatMaster’s numeric parser validates that what remains after removing a recognized currency prefix and thousands separators is actually a clean, properly formed number before accepting it, and returns a null value, exactly as a failed parse should, for anything that is not.

Running an Import

A dataset enters CaatMaster through the Import Data command, which accepts comma-separated files, Excel workbooks of either the legacy or current format, and, for financial statement material specifically, the Financial Import Wizard, which applies additional heuristics suited to a trial balance, a general ledger extract, or a chart of accounts. Where a source workbook contains more than one worksheet, the import prompts for a selection rather than guessing which sheet holds the intended data.

For a financial statement or trial balance import specifically, running the file through the Financial Import Wizard rather than a plain import is worth the additional step. The wizard applies the numeric parsing described above automatically to every column it identifies as likely to be financial, proposes a mapping from the source file’s account labels to the standard concepts used throughout the rest of the application, such as revenue, total assets, or current liabilities, and flags any column where a meaningful share of values failed to parse cleanly, so that the failure is visible before it propagates into a ratio calculation rather than after.

  • From the sidebar, under Import, choose Import Folder Listing or the equivalent Import Data command for a single file, and select ap_transactions.csv, the working file introduced in Chapter 2.
  • CaatMaster reads the file, infers a data type for each of the ten columns, and opens the newly created dataset directly in the Transform view.
  • Give the dataset a clear name, such as AP Transactions, so it can be referred to unambiguously later, including from any dialog that lets a step reference a second dataset.

    • Cleaning What the Import Cannot Fix Alone

    Some data quality issues are not a matter of numeric formatting and require a deliberate cleaning step regardless of how the import itself is handled. A column header that spans two rows in the source spreadsheet, a column that mixes a date format from one region with a date format from another partway down its length, or a row that is actually a subtotal rather than a transaction, are all common enough in real accounting exports that CaatMaster provides a dedicated Cleaning Wizard to surface and resolve them before an analytical test is run against the affected dataset.

    The Cleaning Wizard inspects a freshly imported dataset and proposes a set of corrective steps, each shown with a preview of its effect before it is accepted. As with every other transformation in the application, an accepted cleaning step becomes an ordinary entry in the dataset’s Applied Steps pipeline, and is therefore visible to a second reviewer in exactly the same way a manually applied transformation would be. Every proposed step is tied to an exact, checkable rule rather than a guess; where a judgment call is genuinely required, such as deciding which columns are identifiers rather than values, the wizard proposes the step unchecked, and applies it only if the reviewer actively selects it.

    Interpreting the Result

    When an import produces fewer valid rows than expected

    1. Benign explanation. The source file may genuinely contain blank or non-financial rows, such as section headers or spacing rows carried over from a formatted spreadsheet, which should not have parsed as numeric values in the first place.
    2. Error or judgment lapse. The source system may have exported a column using a numeric convention, such as a regional decimal comma, that the import step was not configured to expect, causing otherwise valid figures to fail parsing.
    3. What would indicate something more serious. A pattern in which specific accounts or specific value ranges consistently fail to parse, rather than a random scattering of blank rows, warrants a direct question to whoever prepared the export about whether the extract itself was filtered or altered before it reached the audit team.

    Chapter 4

    Deterministic Math, AI Where It Belongs

    Artificial intelligence, and specifically the large language models behind CaatMaster’s AI-assisted features, is good at particular kinds of task and poor at others, in ways that are easy to state clearly and important to keep in view throughout the rest of this book. A language model is good at reading unstructured text and extracting the plain-English content of it: identifying what a paragraph in a note to the financial statements is asserting, translating a compliance policy written in prose into a checkable rule, or drafting a description of a finding in professional audit language. A language model is poor at arithmetic performed silently inside its own reasoning, and it is poor in a specific way that matters for an audit tool: it will very often produce an answer that is plausible, confidently stated, and wrong, with no signal to the reader that anything is amiss.

    CaatMaster is built around a single governing rule that follows from this distinction: a calculation that Polars, the deterministic data engine underneath the application, can perform exactly is never delegated to the AI, regardless of how convenient it might be to simply ask a language model for the answer. The AI is used only for the narrower class of task it is actually reliable at, and even there, its output is checked against real data before it is presented as a finding.

    The Two Layers of the Application

    Every calculation in this book that produces a number, whether it is a Benford deviation, a lease liability, or an expected credit loss under IFRS 9, is computed by ordinary, reproducible arithmetic against the complete dataset, using the Polars library. Run the same test twice against the same data and the result is identical to the last decimal place, every time, on every machine. None of these calculations involve a language model at any stage, and none of them can be affected by a change in AI provider, a change in a model’s training, or a network outage.

    A separate layer of the application, described at length in Part VI, uses a language model for tasks that genuinely require reading and producing natural language: summarizing a long narrative disclosure, classifying free-text entries into categories, extracting a list of compliance rules from a written policy document, or drafting the descriptive prose of an audit finding. This layer is deliberately kept away from any task that involves counting, summing, or estimating a quantity, because that is exactly the class of task at which a language model is unreliable in a way that is difficult to detect after the fact.

    Principle

    If a number in a CaatMaster report came from an AI call, something in the design has gone wrong. Every number in this book’s worked examples, and every number CaatMaster itself produces, is traceable to a deterministic calculation against the full population of data, never to a language model’s own arithmetic.

    The Translate-Then-Compute Pattern

    Where an AI-assisted feature does need to interact with real figures, CaatMaster applies a consistent pattern, used throughout the compliance rule extraction feature covered in Chapter 14 and the numeric disclosure reconciliation feature covered in Chapter 25. The language model is asked to translate a piece of unstructured input, such as a sentence of policy text or a paragraph of narrative disclosure, into a structured, checkable statement: a filter condition, or a labeled figure with the sentence it came from. That structured statement is then evaluated against the complete dataset using ordinary code, producing an exact count, an exact dollar amount, and a specific list of the rows involved. Only after this real computation has happened is the language model asked to draft the prose description of the finding, using the real numbers it is given rather than numbers it might otherwise be tempted to estimate.

    This division of labor means the language model is never in a position to simply state that forty percent of transactions violate a policy. It is asked, instead, to say what the policy requires in a form that can be tested, and the forty percent figure, if that turns out to be the correct figure, comes from actually testing every row.

    What This Means When You Read a Finding

    A finding produced entirely by a deterministic test, such as a duplicate payment or a Benford deviation, carries no qualification about its source, because none is needed. A finding whose descriptive text was drafted with AI assistance is marked as such wherever it appears in the application, and the underlying figures behind that description remain fully traceable to the same Applied Steps pipeline described in Chapter 2. An auditor reviewing such a finding should read the drafted prose as a starting point for the workpaper narrative, subject to the same editorial judgment any drafted text would receive, while treating the count, the amount, and the evidence rows as already verified, because they were computed the same way any other number in this book is computed.

    This distinction is worth carrying forward as a standing question to ask of any audit software claiming an AI-assisted feature, CaatMaster included: does a specific number in the output trace back to a real calculation against the complete population, or was it produced, at some point in the chain, by asking a language model what the answer probably is. Where the second is true, the number deserves exactly the scrutiny a rough estimate deserves, no more and no less. Where the first is true, as it is throughout CaatMaster’s analytical library, the number can be relied upon the same way any other output of a well-tested calculation can be relied upon, and the auditor’s attention belongs on interpreting what the number means, not on verifying that it is real.

    Part II

    Classic CAATs

    Chapter 5

    Data Profiling and Descriptive Statistics

    Before any specific audit test is chosen, a reviewer needs a general sense of what the data actually contains. How many rows are there, and how many of them are exact duplicates of one another. How complete is each column, and how many distinct values does it hold. Are there numeric columns whose values spread out in a way that already suggests further inquiry, before a single formal test has been run against them. This general orientation is called profiling, and it belongs at the start of nearly every engagement, not because it produces findings on its own, but because it tells the reviewer where to look next.

    Running the Profile Dataset Command

    CaatMaster provides an automatic profiling command, reached from the sidebar as Profile Dataset, that runs the moment it is invoked against the currently open dataset, without requiring any parameters to be set in advance. The profile examines every column, up to a limit of fifty columns for a very wide dataset, and reports, for each one, its declared data type, the count and percentage of missing values, and the count and percentage of distinct values. For any column recognized as numeric, the profile additionally computes the interquartile range and reports how many of that column’s values fall outside 1.5 times the interquartile range beyond the first and third quartiles, the same fence used throughout this book’s outlier detection chapter.

    The profile goes further than a per-column summary in two respects that make it genuinely useful as a starting point rather than a mechanical listing. First, for every numeric column with at least one hundred non-zero values and enough spread in magnitude to be a plausible amount field, rather than an identifier or a code, the profile computes Mark Nigrini’s mean absolute deviation statistic against Benford’s Law, the same conformity measure used in professional forensic accounting practice, and reports any column whose deviation exceeds the conventional threshold of 0.012, which Nigrini’s own published guidance treats as the boundary between acceptable and marginal conformity. Second, the profile computes the pairwise correlation between every two numeric columns and reports any pair whose correlation, in absolute value, reaches 0.8 or higher, which frequently surfaces the fact that two supposedly independent columns are actually derived from one another, or that a column believed to carry new information is largely redundant with one already understood.

    Every figure the profile reports is computed directly from the data at the moment the command is run. None of it is estimated, inferred, or drawn from a general model of what a typical dataset looks like.

  • With the AP Transactions dataset open, select it in the sidebar dataset list if it is not already the active dataset.
  • Under Analyze in the sidebar, click Profile Dataset. No parameters are required; the command runs immediately against the dataset’s current state.
  • Review the summary tiles at the top of the resulting dialog, then scroll the Column Profile table for any row whose Missing, Unique, or Outliers percentage stands out.

    • Field Statistics: A Deeper Descriptive Layer

    Where the automatic profile gives a fast overview, the Field Statistics operation, found in the Transform view under the statistics category, produces a considerably more detailed report and, unlike the sidebar profile command, becomes a recorded step in the dataset’s Applied Steps pipeline, which means it can be saved and reproduced against a later extract of the same data. For every selected column, or every column in the dataset if none are specifically selected, Field Statistics reports the count, the missing count and percentage, and the number of distinct values, matching the automatic profile. For numeric columns, it goes considerably further, reporting the minimum, maximum, range, and sum, the mean and median, the sample standard deviation and variance, skewness and kurtosis where the column has enough values to compute them meaningfully, the fifth, twenty-fifth, fiftieth, seventy-fifth, and ninety-fifth percentiles, and the coefficient of variation, which expresses the standard deviation as a proportion of the mean and allows the spread of columns measured in different units to be compared on a common footing. Every column, numeric or not, additionally reports its most frequently occurring value and how often it occurs, alongside the least frequently occurring value.

    Skewness and kurtosis deserve a brief explanation for a reader who has not encountered them before. Skewness measures whether a distribution leans further in one direction than the other around its center; a strongly positive skew in an expense account, for example, suggests a small number of unusually large transactions pulling the distribution’s tail to the right, which is itself worth investigating. Kurtosis measures how much of a distribution’s variance comes from occasional extreme values relative to frequent, modest ones; a distribution with high kurtosis warns a reviewer that summary statistics such as the mean are being disproportionately influenced by a small number of large transactions rather than describing the typical case.

    A scenario worth recognizing

    Suppose a reviewer opens a newly imported accounts payable extract of eighteen thousand rows and runs Profile Dataset before deciding which tests to prioritize. The profile reports that the Vendor ID column is ninety-nine point four percent complete, which is unremarkable, but that the Approval Date column is only sixty-one percent complete, meaning close to seven thousand payments carry no recorded approval date at all. The profile also reports that the Payment Amount column shows a Benford deviation of 0.021, above the 0.012 conformity threshold, and that Payment Amount and Invoice Amount correlate at 0.97, which is expected for two columns that should nearly always match, but is worth confirming rather than assuming.

    None of these three observations is, by itself, a finding severe enough to report. Together, they tell the reviewer where the engagement’s substantive testing should concentrate: a completeness test on Approval Date, described in the next chapter, and a closer Benford’s Law analysis on Payment Amount, described in Chapter 8, are now the natural next steps rather than an arbitrary starting point chosen without evidence.

    Interpreting the Result

    When a profile surfaces an unusual pattern

    1. Benign explanation. A high missing-value percentage in a specific column often reflects a field that a source system only began populating partway through the period under review, or a field that is genuinely optional for a subset of legitimate transaction types.
    2. Error or judgment lapse. A near-perfect correlation between two columns that ought to carry independent information can indicate that one column was populated by copying the other during data entry, rather than being independently recorded, which weakens any control that assumes the two values were determined separately.
    3. What would indicate something more serious. A missing-value pattern concentrated in transactions above a specific dollar threshold, rather than spread evenly across the population, suggests the missing field was deliberately left blank to avoid triggering a review step tied to that field, and warrants a direct conversation with the process owner.

    Chapter 6

    Completeness and Integrity

    A ratio, a trend, or a statistical test built on top of a column that is silently incomplete produces a number that is technically calculated correctly and substantively wrong, because it describes only the subset of the population that happened to have a value recorded. Completeness and integrity testing exists to establish, before any other analysis proceeds, whether a column actually contains what it is supposed to contain, across the whole population, and to quantify exactly how far short of that standard it falls where it does not.

    The Six Verification Checks

    CaatMaster’s Verify Data command applies one or more named checks to selected columns and returns a report, one row per check, rather than modifying the underlying dataset in any way. Six check types are available. A numeric check confirms that every non-null value in a column genuinely parses as a number, using the same validated parsing logic described in Chapter 3, and reports how many values fail to do so. A date check performs the equivalent test for date values. A no-nulls check simply counts how many null values a column contains, which is the most direct completeness test available. A unique check counts how many values in a column occur more than once, appropriate for any column that is supposed to serve as an identifier, such as an invoice number or an employee ID. A positive check counts how many values in a numeric column are zero or negative, useful for columns such as quantity or unit price that should never fall to zero or below under normal business circumstances. An in-range check counts how many values fall outside an auditor-specified minimum and maximum, useful for a column such as a discount percentage that has a defined valid range regardless of what the data happens to contain.

    Each check reports a fail count, a plain status of pass, fail, or skipped, and a short description of what was found. A check is marked skipped, rather than failed, when the requested check cannot meaningfully apply to the column’s actual data type, such as a positive-value check requested against a text column; this distinction matters because a skipped check should prompt the reviewer to reconsider whether the check was configured correctly, while a failed check is a positive finding in its own right.

    Running a Verification

    The Verify Data dialog allows any number of checks to be assembled against any combination of columns in a single pass, producing one consolidated report rather than requiring each check to be run and reviewed separately. A typical completeness pass against a general ledger extract, for example, would combine a no-nulls check against the account code, the posting date, and the amount columns, a unique check against the journal entry number, and a positive check against the amount column if the ledger convention in use records debits and credits as separate signed columns rather than a single unsigned amount with a type indicator.

  • Under Analyze in the sidebar, click Verify Data to open the dialog against the active dataset.
  • In the Add Expectation row, set Column to approver and Check to no_nulls, then click + Add.
  • Repeat for Column invoice_id with Check unique, and again for Column amount with Check positive. All three now appear in the Expectations To Check table.
  • Click Run Verification. The Results table below populates with one row per check.

    • The result matches what a direct inspection of the working file would show: five of the thirty-four records carry no approver, a fourteen point seven percent gap. Every invoice ID is unique and every amount is strictly positive, so those two checks pass without qualification.

    A scenario worth recognizing

    Consider a payroll extract of four thousand two hundred employee records submitted ahead of a compensation review. A no-nulls check against the Employee ID, Base Salary, and Department columns reports zero failures on all three, which might reasonably be read as a clean population. A unique check against Employee ID, however, reports eleven duplicate occurrences, meaning eleven employee identifiers appear more than once in the file. On inspection, each duplicated identifier corresponds to an employee who transferred between departments mid-period and was exported once under each department’s payroll run, rather than once under a single consolidated record.

    A reviewer who accepted the no-nulls result alone and moved directly to a compensation-by-department analysis would have counted each of these eleven employees twice, inflating the department headcount and, depending on how the analysis aggregated pay, potentially double-counting their compensation as well. The uniqueness check is what surfaces a completeness problem that a nulls check, on its own, cannot detect, since none of the affected fields were actually missing a value.

    Interpreting the Result

    When a verification check reports failures

    1. Benign explanation. A field may legitimately be blank for a specific transaction type, such as a discount percentage on an invoice that carries no discount, and a no-nulls failure on that field may simply reflect an overly broad check rather than a real data quality problem.
    2. Error or judgment lapse. A recurring duplicate identifier, as in the payroll example above, more often reflects a limitation in how a source system exports data under a specific business event, such as a mid-period transfer, than any intent to misstate the underlying records.
    3. What would indicate something more serious. A pattern of missing or duplicated values concentrated among a specific approver, vendor, or account, rather than distributed in a way consistent with the stated benign explanation, warrants direct follow-up with whoever controls that segment of the process.

    Chapter 7

    Cross-Tabulation and Grouping

    Many of the questions an audit actually needs answered are not about a single column in isolation, but about how two attributes relate to one another across a population. Do refunds cluster among a small number of employees. Does a particular approval status appear disproportionately often for a particular vendor. A cross-tabulation, sometimes called a contingency table, answers exactly this kind of question by counting, or aggregating, how often each combination of two categorical values occurs together.

    Running a Cross-Tabulation

    The Cross-Tabulation operation, found in the Transform view under the statistics category, takes a row variable and a column variable, both categorical, and produces a table with one row per distinct value of the row variable and one column per distinct value of the column variable. By default, each cell in the resulting table counts how many records share that particular combination of row and column values. An optional value column and aggregation function, chosen from sum, mean, minimum, or maximum, replace the count with an aggregate of a numeric column instead, which turns the same structural device into a tool for comparing, for example, total transaction value by employee and by transaction type, rather than merely the number of transactions.

    An optional percentage display recasts each cell as a percentage rather than a raw count or aggregate, and this option accepts a choice of denominator: a percentage of the table’s grand total, a percentage within each row, or a percentage within each column. This choice changes the question the table actually answers, and choosing incorrectly is one of the more common ways a cross-tabulation is misread. A percentage of the row total answers what share of a given employee’s transactions fall into each category; a percentage of the column total answers what share of a given category’s transactions belong to each employee. The two are not the same, and confusing them can lead a reviewer to describe a finding in a way that overstates or understates its actual significance.

    Cross-Tabulation has no button in the sidebar, but it is reachable two ways: from the top menu bar’s Statistics menu, or the way most of CaatMaster’s deeper analytical operations can also be reached, by right-clicking directly on a column header in the data grid. This chapter uses the right-click path, since it is the one that generalizes to the largest number of operations covered in this book.

  • In the Transform view, right-click the header of any column in the AP Transactions dataset. A menu opens with quick actions at the top (Sort, Remove, Visualize) followed by every operation in the application, grouped into submenus that mirror the top menu bar’s categories, including a Statistics and a Financial submenu; a handful of operations under each, covered individually across this book, are additionally promoted to their own top menu bar entries, but most of the right-click catalog still has no other path.
  • Choose Statistics → Cross-Tabulation.... Which column was right-clicked does not matter; the dialog that opens lets any column be chosen for any role.
  • Set Row Variable to department and Column Variable to status.
  • Set Value Column to amount and Aggregation Function to sum, so each cell totals dollar value rather than counting transactions.
  • Click Generate Crosstab.

    A scenario worth recognizing

    Suppose an accounts payable team wants to understand whether payment approvals are concentrated among too few individuals for the volume of transactions being approved. A cross-tabulation with Approver as the row variable and Payment Method as the column variable, aggregating on Payment Amount with a sum function, shows that one approver, out of fourteen active approvers, accounts for sixty-two percent of all wire transfer value for the period, expressed as a percentage of the column total.

    Read as a percentage of that approver’s own row instead, the same underlying data might show that wire transfers make up only eighteen percent of that individual’s total approval volume, meaning the concentration is specific to the wire transfer payment method rather than reflecting an approver who dominates approvals in general. Both readings are correct; they answer different questions, and a workpaper narrative needs to state clearly which one is being reported, since a reader who assumes the other interpretation could draw a materially different conclusion about the severity of the concentration.

    Interpreting the Result

    When a cross-tabulation shows concentration in one cell

    1. Benign explanation. A single approver or employee may legitimately handle a disproportionate share of one transaction type because of role assignment, seniority, or regional responsibility, rather than any control weakness.
    2. Error or judgment lapse. Concentration can also result from a workflow tool that defaults every transaction of a given type to a single approver’s queue, regardless of that approver’s intended authority, which is a control design issue rather than an individual’s action.
    3. What would indicate something more serious. Concentration that coincides with the same individual having originated or requested the underlying transactions, rather than merely approved them, raises a segregation of duties question addressed directly in Chapter 12.

    Chapter 8

    Benford’s Law

    Benford’s Law describes an observation, first published by the physicist Frank Benford in 1938 and later brought into forensic accounting practice by Mark Nigrini, that in many naturally occurring collections of numbers, the leading digit is not uniformly distributed across the values one through nine. The digit one appears as the leading digit roughly thirty percent of the time, the digit nine appears as the leading digit less than five percent of the time, and the frequencies of the digits in between decline steadily according to a logarithmic formula. This pattern holds for collections of numbers that span several orders of magnitude and arise from an unconstrained natural process, such as transaction amounts across a large general ledger, and tends to break down for numbers that are artificially constrained, such as prices deliberately set just under a round figure, or numbers that are assigned rather than measured, such as invoice numbers or telephone extensions.

    The value of Benford’s Law to an auditor lies in its use as a screening test. A dataset of transaction amounts that conforms closely to the expected distribution provides mild comfort that the values were not extensively fabricated by a person choosing numbers that felt plausible, since people are demonstrably poor at manufacturing numbers with the correct leading-digit frequencies. A dataset that deviates substantially from the expected distribution does not, on its own, prove fabrication; it indicates that the population is worth a closer look, using the more targeted techniques described elsewhere in this book.

    Two Ways CaatMaster Applies This Test

    CaatMaster applies Benford’s Law in two distinct places, at two distinct levels of granularity, and the difference between them matters for how each is used. The automatic Profile Dataset command, described in Chapter 5, applies a whole-column conformity test: it computes Nigrini’s mean absolute deviation statistic for a candidate amount column and reports whether that single summary number exceeds the 0.012 threshold treated in Nigrini’s published guidance as the boundary of acceptable conformity. This is a fast, automatic screen that answers one question: does this column, taken as a whole, look like the kind of population Benford’s Law would predict.

    The dedicated Benford’s Law Analysis operation, found in the Transform view, answers a more granular question and is the tool to reach for once the whole-column screen has indicated that a closer look is warranted. It computes, for every row, the value’s leading digit or, optionally, its leading two digits, adds that digit as a new column, and then computes two further columns: the frequency with which that specific leading digit actually occurs across the whole dataset, and the absolute difference between that actual frequency and the frequency Benford’s Law predicts for it. Because this deviation is attached to every row individually, a reviewer can sort or filter the dataset by deviation and go directly to the transactions carrying the most overrepresented leading digits, rather than working only with a single column-level verdict.

    Running a Benford’s Law Analysis

    Selecting the operation requires only a numeric column to analyze. An option to analyze the leading two digits rather than the leading one digit narrows the test considerably, since the two-digit version compares against ninety possible values, from ten through ninety-nine, rather than nine, and is appropriate once a population is large enough, generally several thousand values or more, to populate each of those ninety buckets meaningfully. A further option restricts the digit extraction to a value’s significant digits only, which matters for a column recorded to a fixed number of decimal places, where the digits immediately after a decimal point would otherwise be treated as leading digits in a way that does not reflect the underlying magnitude of the transaction.

  • From the top menu bar, choose Audit → Audit Checks → Benford’s Law Analysis.... The same dialog is also reachable by right-clicking any column header and choosing Audit → Benford’s Law Analysis... from the full operation menu described in Chapter 7; the top menu bar simply promotes this operation, along with the rest of the Audit Checks group, to a permanent, one-click location since it is used so frequently.
  • Set Column to Analyze to amount and leave Leading Digits at its default of 1 (First digit only).
  • Click Run Analysis.

    • Run against the thirty-four-row AP Transactions working file, this last step does not produce a chart. It produces a warning.

    To show what a completed analysis looks like, the screenshot below runs the same dialog against a larger, separately generated population of five hundred transaction amounts built to resemble the kind of spread a real accounts payable ledger would show. This population exists only to illustrate the technique at a workable scale and is not part of the working file introduced in Chapter 2.

    A scenario worth recognizing

    Suppose a procurement audit runs the two-digit Benford analysis against a purchase order value column of nine thousand records. The result shows the leading digits forty-nine and ninety-nine occurring far more often than Benford’s Law predicts, at frequencies roughly three times the expected rate, while every other leading two-digit combination sits close to its expected frequency. A reviewer filtering the dataset to purchase orders beginning with these two digit combinations finds that the great majority of them fall just under two internal approval thresholds set at five thousand dollars and ten thousand dollars, meaning the actual values cluster near four thousand nine hundred and nine thousand nine hundred.

    This is precisely the pattern Benford’s Law is best at surfacing: values that are not randomly generated but deliberately positioned just beneath a control threshold, whether to avoid a required second approval or simply because a requester rounded down from a mental estimate of the threshold without any intent to circumvent it. The Benford test cannot distinguish between these two explanations on its own; it can only point to where the concentration lies.

    Limits of the Technique

    A leading-digit test is not appropriate for every numeric column, and applying it indiscriminately produces false alarms that waste review time. Columns that are assigned rather than measured, such as invoice numbers, employee identifiers, or check numbers, do not follow Benford’s Law and should not be tested against it. Columns with an artificially narrow range, such as a discount percentage that can only take values between zero and twenty, likewise fall outside the conditions under which the law is expected to hold. Nigrini’s own published guidance treats several hundred values as the practical minimum for a reliable result; CaatMaster enforces a stricter floor directly in the dialog, refusing to run the dedicated Benford’s Law Analysis operation at all below one hundred valid, non-zero values, as Figure 8.1 shows. A reviewer working with a smaller population is not without options: the population can be widened, for instance by extending the period under review, or the test can be deferred until enough transactions have accumulated to apply it meaningfully.

    Interpreting the Result

    When a column deviates from the expected distribution

    1. Benign explanation. A column that mixes several genuinely different populations, such as invoice amounts from two business units with very different average transaction sizes, can deviate from Benford’s Law even though neither population, considered on its own, is unusual.
    2. Error or judgment lapse. Values clustered just under a threshold, as in the case above, more often reflect informal rounding by requesters familiar with an approval limit than deliberate structuring, particularly where the clustering is broad and involves many different individuals.
    3. What would indicate something more serious. Clustering concentrated among a small number of requesters or approvers, rather than spread broadly across the population, together with values that fall just barely under the threshold rather than comfortably under it, is the pattern most consistent with deliberate avoidance of a control and warrants direct inquiry.

    Chapter 9

    Ratio and Trend Analysis

    A single financial figure, taken alone, rarely tells an auditor very much. Revenue of forty-two million dollars is neither large nor small without a point of comparison. A ratio supplies that point of comparison by relating one figure to another in a way that is meaningful regardless of the absolute size of the business being examined, and a trend supplies a second kind of comparison by relating a figure to its own past values over time. Chapter 3 addressed the precondition both techniques depend on: a ratio or a trend calculated from a badly parsed numerator or denominator is worse than no ratio at all, because it carries the appearance of precision without the substance of it.

    The Working Financial Dataset

    This chapter introduces the second recurring dataset used in this book, alongside the accounts payable extract from Chapter 2. The file, quarterly_financials.csv, holds four rows, one per quarter of Meridian Office Supply Co.’s 2024 fiscal year, already arranged in the wide, one-row-per-period layout that CaatMaster’s ratio calculation expects, with a separate column for each concept: revenue, cost of goods sold, gross profit, net income, EBITDA, current assets, current liabilities, cash, inventory, total assets, total liabilities, total equity, and interest expense. A statement exported in the more common long format, one row per account per period, is brought into this shape first using the Reshape Statement to Ratio Inputs operation, or through the mapping step built into the Financial Import Wizard from Chapter 3.

    The Four Families of Ratio

    CaatMaster’s Financial Ratios feature groups its calculations into four families, labeled in the dialog itself as Liquidity, Solvency, Profitability, and Efficiency, matching the categories used throughout financial statement analysis generally. Liquidity ratios, comprising the current ratio, the quick ratio, and the cash ratio, measure a company’s capacity to meet short-term obligations as they come due, each one progressively stricter about which current assets it counts as available to do so. Solvency ratios, comprising the debt-to-equity ratio, the debt ratio, and interest coverage, measure how heavily a company relies on borrowed funds relative to its own capital, and how comfortably its earnings cover the interest expense that borrowing creates. Profitability ratios, comprising net profit margin, gross margin, return on assets, return on equity, and EBITDA margin, measure how effectively a company converts revenue and assets into earnings. Efficiency ratios, represented in the current release by asset turnover, measure how effectively a company uses its asset base to generate revenue.

    Every ratio in every family is calculated with the same safeguard described in Chapter 3: a denominator of exactly zero produces a genuinely missing result rather than an unbounded or undefined number silently propagating into every calculation and chart that later depends on it. A reviewer examining a ratio report and finding a blank value where a ratio would normally appear should read that blank as an honest signal that the denominator was zero for that period or entity, not as a defect in the calculation.

    One formula is worth stating precisely rather than left to assumption, since it departs from the version printed in most introductory textbooks. Interest coverage in CaatMaster is calculated as net income plus interest expense, divided by interest expense, rather than the more common earnings-before-interest-and-tax divided by interest expense. Because net income has already had tax deducted from it, this version of the ratio runs somewhat lower than the textbook formula would produce from the same underlying figures. A reviewer citing this figure in a workpaper should describe it as calculated, not assume it matches a number pulled from a different source without checking the formula behind it.

    Running a Ratio Analysis

    Calculating a ratio in CaatMaster begins with mapping the standard financial concepts each ratio depends on, such as current assets, current liabilities, or net income, to the actual column names present in the imported dataset. Where a financial statement was brought in through the Financial Import Wizard described in Chapter 3, or through the XBRL import pipeline described in Chapter 22, this mapping is proposed automatically based on the recognized concept and can be adjusted before any ratio is calculated.
