    Three Further Analyses

    The Financial Ratios dialog offers three additional analyses beyond the twelve core ratios. Vertical analysis, sometimes called common-size analysis, restates every line item as a percentage of a chosen base figure, typically revenue for an income statement or total assets for a balance sheet, which allows statements of very different sizes to be compared directly. Horizontal analysis restates each line item as a percentage change from a chosen base period, which is a more formal, statement-wide counterpart to the period-by-period Trend Analysis described later in this chapter.

    The Altman Z-Score is a bankruptcy-risk model, developed by Edward Altman in 1968 and still in wide professional use, that combines five weighted ratios, working capital to total assets, retained earnings to total assets, earnings before interest and tax to total assets, equity to total liabilities, and revenue to total assets, into a single score, with separate coefficient sets and interpretation thresholds depending on whether the company being assessed is publicly traded. Two aspects of CaatMaster’s implementation deserve a direct note of caution. If retained earnings is not separately mapped, the calculation substitutes one-half of total equity as a rough estimate, rather than leaving the ratio blank. If a distinct earnings-before-interest-and-tax figure is not mapped, the calculation substitutes EBITDA in its place, which is consistently higher than EBIT and therefore biases the score toward the safer end of its scale. A reviewer relying on the Z-Score for a genuine going-concern assessment should confirm that both retained earnings and EBIT, not EBITDA, were mapped explicitly, rather than accept the fallback values without checking.

    Trend Analysis Across Periods

    Trend Analysis takes a date column and a value column and aggregates the value by calendar period, using day, week, month, quarter, or year as the grouping unit, with a choice of sum, mean, count, minimum, or maximum as the aggregation applied within each period. This produces a compact time series suitable for charting through the Visualizations view covered in Chapter 27, and is the appropriate first step whenever a question concerns change over time rather than a single point-in-time comparison, such as whether a particular expense category has been growing faster than revenue over successive quarters.

    Grouping the Inventory column of quarterly_financials.csv by quarter and summing within each period shows inventory rising from 210,000 in the first quarter to 305,000 in the fourth, an increase of forty-five percent, while the same grouping applied to Revenue shows growth of only five percent over the same four quarters. This is precisely the pattern behind the widening gap between the current ratio and the quick ratio in Figure 9.2: inventory, not a broad decline across every current asset, is what is pulling working capital down.

    A scenario worth recognizing

    Suppose a working capital review extends the same kind of analysis shown in Figure 9.2 across eight quarters rather than four, for a distributor considerably larger than Meridian Office Supply Co. The current ratio, calculated the same way, declines steadily from 1.85 to 1.12 over that period, while the quick ratio declines much more sharply, from 1.20 to 0.58. Because the quick ratio excludes inventory from current assets while the current ratio includes it, the gap widening between the two ratios points specifically at inventory as the driver of the decline, rather than a broad deterioration across every current asset category, exactly as in the four-quarter working example above but at a scale severe enough to warrant a formal finding.

    A trend analysis of the Inventory column alone, grouped by quarter, confirms that inventory has grown forty-one percent over the same eight quarters while revenue, aggregated over the same periods, grew only six percent. Inventory accumulating well ahead of the sales activity needed to justify it is a classic indicator worth investigating further, whether the underlying cause turns out to be a genuine demand slowdown that management has not yet reflected in a valuation allowance, a data entry issue overstating quantities on hand, or slow-moving stock that should have been written down under the analysis covered in Chapter 19.

    Interpreting the Result

    When a ratio or a trend moves outside its expected range

    1. Benign explanation. A ratio can move because of a genuine, disclosed business change, such as a planned inventory build ahead of a known seasonal peak, that has nothing to do with reporting quality.
    2. Error or judgment lapse. A sudden, isolated jump in a ratio between two adjacent periods, rather than a gradual trend, often traces back to a misclassification between two account categories, such as a current asset booked as non-current, rather than a change in the underlying business.
    3. What would indicate something more serious. A ratio that moves gradually in a direction management has strong incentive to avoid disclosing, such as a debt covenant ratio drifting toward its contractual limit over several consecutive periods without any corresponding management commentary, warrants direct inquiry into why the trend has not been addressed.

    Chapter 10

    Outlier and Anomaly Detection

    An outlier is a value that sits meaningfully apart from the rest of its population, and detecting one is only useful once a reviewer has settled on a defensible definition of how far apart is meaningful. CaatMaster offers two statistically grounded definitions for a quick, single-column screen, a dedicated round-number test aimed at a specific and well-documented manipulation pattern, and a set of trainable machine learning models for anomaly detection that considers more than one column of context at a time.

    Two Statistical Definitions of Unusual

    The interquartile range method defines the bulk of a population as the range between its first and third quartiles, and flags any value falling more than one and a half times that range below the first quartile or above the third as an outlier, the same convention, sometimes called Tukey’s fences, used in the box plots taught in most introductory statistics courses. This method has the advantage of being resistant to the outliers themselves distorting the boundary, since quartiles are not pulled by extreme values the way a mean is.

    The z-score method instead measures how many standard deviations a value sits from the population mean, and flags a value once that count exceeds a chosen threshold, three standard deviations in CaatMaster’s default configuration. This method is more familiar to most reviewers but is itself sensitive to extreme values, because a small number of very large outliers can inflate the standard deviation enough to mask their own significance, and a population with a strongly skewed distribution, common in financial data where amounts cannot be negative and often span several orders of magnitude, tends to overstate how many values legitimately belong in the tail. In practice, the interquartile range method is the more conservative and generally preferable choice for financial transaction data, and the z-score method is better suited to data that is closer to normally distributed by nature, such as a physical measurement or a well-behaved ratio.

    Running Outlier Detection

    Audit Outlier Detection, found in the Transform view under the audit category, requires a column and a choice of method, and adds a boolean flag column together with a column recording how far each flagged value deviates from the applicable boundary, expressed in units of the interquartile range for the interquartile range method or in standard deviations for the z-score method. Because both flag and deviation columns become ordinary columns in the dataset, they can be sorted, filtered, or combined with other criteria using any of the general-purpose transformations available elsewhere in the application.

  • From the top menu bar, choose Audit → Audit Checks → Outlier Detection... against the AP Transactions dataset. As with Benford’s Law, the same dialog is also reachable by right-clicking a column header and choosing Audit → Outlier Detection.
  • Set Column to amount and Method to iqr.
  • Leave Flag Column and Deviation Column at their defaults, is_outlier and outlier_deviation.
  • Click OK. The two new columns appear immediately in the data grid.
    • InvoiceVendorAmountDeviation (in IQR)
    20010Cascade IT Solutions9,900.002.70
    20034Harborview Consulting10,000.002.80
    20027Cascade IT Solutions48,750.0041.55

    Figure 10.2 — The three rows flagged by the interquartile range method against ap_transactions.csv. The server rack cooling fan invoice deviates more than forty-one interquartile ranges beyond the upper fence, an order of magnitude past the other two.

    Round Number Detection

    A cluster of unusually round transaction amounts is a long-recognized indicator worth checking for in its own right, since genuine transaction amounts, arrived at through pricing calculations, tax computations, and negotiated terms, tend to include cents and non-round dollar figures, while amounts entered by estimation, or fabricated without reference to an underlying calculation, disproportionately land on round figures. Round Number Detection scores each value in a column by the proportion of its digits that are trailing zeros, so that a value of five thousand, three of whose four digits are trailing zeros, scores 0.75, while a value of one hundred fifty scores approximately 0.33, and any value carrying a fractional cent amount scores zero regardless of how round its whole-dollar portion might look. A configurable threshold, set to 0.9 by default, determines how round a value must be before it is flagged.

    Round Number Detection is reached the same way as the two operations above it in this chapter: Audit → Audit Checks → Round Number Analysis on the top menu bar, or the equivalent entry in a column header’s right-click menu. This default threshold is calibrated with large balances in mind and should be lowered for a population of smaller transaction amounts. By construction, a four-digit whole-dollar amount can score at most 0.75, since its leading digit can never be a trailing zero, and a five-digit amount can score at most 0.8; neither could ever reach the default 0.9 threshold regardless of how round it looks to a human reviewer. Run against ap_transactions.csv with the threshold lowered to 0.7, Round Number Detection flags two records: invoice 20007, five thousand dollars even, scoring 0.75, and invoice 20034, ten thousand dollars even, scoring 0.8. Both belong to the same vendor, Harborview Consulting, which on its own is not yet a finding, but is exactly the kind of pattern worth a closer look at that vendor’s invoicing history.

    Machine Learning Anomaly Models

    The top menu bar’s ML menu includes an Anomaly Detection submenu offering Isolation Forest, Z-Score, IQR, and LOF as one-click options. All four now run the genuine algorithm their name promises: Isolation Forest and LOF call directly into the scikit-learn library’s own IsolationForest and LocalOutlierFactor implementations against the single chosen column, rather than an internal stand-in. An earlier version of this submenu scored both by distance from the column mean, a method closer to the z-score technique described earlier in this chapter than to true isolation-based or density-based detection, which a reviewer selecting Isolation Forest by name had no way to know from the interface alone; that gap is closed, and every value these two entries produce, the anomaly flag and its underlying score, now comes from the real algorithm.

    What still separates this submenu from the trainable models described next is scope, not authenticity. Each entry here considers exactly one column at a time: LOF, for instance, judges a value anomalous by comparing the local density of its own neighborhood against its neighbors’ neighborhoods within that single column, which is genuine density-based reasoning but necessarily blind to any pattern that only shows up across several columns at once. The genuine, multivariate versions live in a separate part of the application, reached from the top menu bar through ML → Model Tools → Train Model..., which opens a dedicated training dialog rather than adding a single Applied Step. This workflow supports training an anomaly detection model across several columns at once, using the same scikit-learn library’s established implementations of Isolation Forest, Local Outlier Factor, and One-Class Support Vector Machine. Unlike the single-column entries in the ML menu’s Anomaly Detection submenu, these models can surface a transaction that looks unremarkable in every individual field but unusual in the combination of fields taken together, such as a transaction whose amount, time of day, and approver are each ordinary on their own but rarely occur together. A trained model can be saved and applied again to a later extract of comparable data, which makes this the appropriate technique for a recurring monitoring program rather than a one-time review.

    A scenario worth recognizing

    Suppose a travel and expense review applies interquartile range outlier detection to a Claim Amount column of six thousand two hundred expense claims and flags one hundred forty of them as statistical outliers. Reviewing these flagged claims individually, the majority turn out to be legitimate, larger claims tied to international travel, easily explained by higher costs in the visited location. Separately, the same reviewer trains an Isolation Forest model across four columns at once, Claim Amount, Day of Week, Time Submitted, and Employee Department, and this model flags a much smaller set of nineteen claims, none of which were flagged by the single-column outlier test, because no individual field value was unusual. What these nineteen claims share is an unusual combination: each was submitted on a weekend, for an amount just under the two-hundred-dollar receipt-exemption threshold, by an employee in a department with no recorded weekend business activity.

    The two techniques answered different questions and found different things, which is the reason CaatMaster offers both rather than treating one as a replacement for the other.

    Interpreting the Result

    When a value or a record is flagged as anomalous

    1. Benign explanation. A statistically unusual value very often corresponds to a genuinely unusual, but entirely legitimate, business event, such as a one-time bulk purchase or an executive’s international travel claim.
    2. Error or judgment lapse. A round-number cluster can result from a policy of entering estimated amounts pending a final invoice, later corrected, rather than any attempt to misstate a balance permanently.
    3. What would indicate something more serious. A pattern of anomalies clustered around a single individual, timing window, or combination of attributes chosen specifically to avoid a documented control threshold, as in the weekend claims example above, warrants direct inquiry rather than dismissal as statistical noise.

    Chapter 11

    Sampling and Stratification

    Most of the techniques covered so far in this book examine an entire population at once, which is one of the principal advantages a computer-assisted audit technique holds over traditional manual testing. Sampling remains necessary all the same, whether because a specific test, such as a physical inspection or a third-party confirmation, cannot practically be performed on every item in a population, or because a statistically valid projection of a sample’s results is itself the form of evidence a particular audit objective calls for. CaatMaster treats sampling as a three-stage discipline: planning how large a sample needs to be, selecting the specific items that make up the sample, and, once the sample has been examined, projecting its results back onto the full population with a defined level of statistical confidence.

    Planning a Sample Size

    Classical variables sample size planning answers a specific question: given an estimate of how much the population’s values vary, expressed as a standard deviation, how large a sample is required to estimate the population’s total value within a chosen tolerable precision, at a chosen confidence level. This is a standalone tool, separate from the operation catalog described in Chapter 7, and is reached from the sidebar rather than from any menu: under Analyze, click Variables Sampling to open the Classical Variables Sampling dialog, which holds sample size planning and sample evaluation as two tabs of the same window.

    CaatMaster’s sample size calculation follows the standard mean-per-unit formula taught in AICPA audit sampling guidance, taking the population size, an estimated population standard deviation drawn from a pilot sample or a prior period’s results, the desired confidence level, and the tolerable precision as inputs, and applying a finite population correction that reduces the required sample size once the sample would otherwise represent a substantial share of a small population. A confidence level of ninety-five percent, the most commonly used standard in audit practice, corresponds to a fixed multiplier of 1.960 in the underlying formula; CaatMaster looks this value up directly for the confidence levels most commonly used in practice and computes it from the normal distribution for any other confidence level requested.

  • From the sidebar, under Analyze, click Variables Sampling.
  • On the Calculate Sample Size tab, enter Population Size 2100, Estimated Population Std Dev 380, Confidence Level 95, and Tolerable Precision 150000.
  • Click Calculate Sample Size.

    • Selecting the Sample

    Sample size planning determines how many items to select; a separate dialog determines which specific items those are. This dialog, labeled Sampling, has no button in the sidebar; it is reached, like Cross-Tabulation and Financial Ratios, by right-clicking a column header and choosing Statistics → Sampling..., or from the top menu bar’s own Statistics menu. It offers four selection methods. Random sampling draws a specified number of rows from the population with each row equally likely to be selected, using a specified seed value where the selection needs to be reproducible for a second reviewer. Systematic sampling selects every kth row starting from a random point within the first interval, which is faster to explain and defend than pure random selection but assumes the population carries no periodic pattern that could coincide with the chosen interval. Stratified sampling divides the population into groups based on a chosen column, such as region or transaction type, and draws a number of items from each group in proportion to that group’s share of the population, which ensures that smaller but potentially important segments of the population are not overlooked entirely by chance the way pure random sampling might overlook them. The fourth method, monetary unit sampling, is the technique most specific to a financial statement audit and is given a full walkthrough below.

    Monetary Unit Sampling

    Rather than treating each row as an equally likely sampling unit, monetary unit sampling, also known as dollar-unit or probability-proportional-to-size sampling, treats each individual dollar of value as the sampling unit, so that a row recording one hundred thousand dollars is one hundred times more likely to be selected than a row recording one thousand dollars. CaatMaster implements this by cumulating the absolute value of the chosen value column across the population, dividing the total by the desired sample size to establish a fixed sampling interval, choosing a single random starting point within that interval, and then selecting every row whose position in the cumulative total falls at the starting point or at each subsequent multiple of the interval beyond it.

    Because larger items are proportionally more likely to be selected under this method, any item whose own value exceeds the sampling interval is guaranteed selection, sometimes at more than one selection point if the item is large enough to span several intervals; CaatMaster records how many selection points each selected item absorbed, so a reviewer can see directly which items were examined because of their sheer size rather than through the ordinary probability mechanism. This property, guaranteed coverage of the largest items in a population, is precisely why monetary unit sampling has been the dominant substantive sampling method in financial statement auditing for decades: an error concealed in a small transaction can only ever cause a small misstatement, while an error concealed in a very large transaction is exactly the kind of item this method ensures gets examined.

  • Right-click any column header in the AP Transactions dataset and choose Statistics → Sampling....
  • Under Sampling Method, select Monetary Unit Sample (MUS/PPS).
  • Under Sample Size, select Fixed number of rows and enter 8.
  • Set Value column (dollar amount) to amount, and Random Seed to 7 so the selection can be reproduced by a second reviewer.
  • Click Generate Sample.
    • InvoiceVendorAmountSelection Points Absorbed
    20002Cascade IT Solutions1,290.001
    20008Anderson Paper Co842.501
    20014GreenLeaf Catering2,500.001
    20022Evergreen Facilities3,210.151
    20027Cascade IT Solutions48,750.003
    20030Fenwick Legal Group3,320.001

    Figure 11.2 — The result of the eight-point selection above. Six physical invoices cover the eight selection points, because the 48,750.00 server rack cooling fan invoice, the same outlier identified in Chapter 10, is large enough on its own to absorb three points. It would have been selected under this method regardless of the random seed chosen, which is exactly the guarantee monetary unit sampling is designed to provide.

    Evaluating a Sample’s Results

    Once a sample has been drawn and each selected item has been examined against its supporting evidence, producing both the originally recorded, or book, value and the verified, or audited, value for each item, the Evaluate Sample Results tab of the same Classical Variables Sampling dialog used for size planning projects those results back onto the full population. Three estimation methods are available. Mean-per-unit estimation projects the sample’s average audited value across the entire population and is the simplest to explain, though the least precise of the three where book values are already known. Difference estimation projects the sample’s average difference between audited and book value across the population and adds that projected difference to the population’s known book total, which produces a considerably more precise estimate whenever errors tend to be roughly similar in dollar size regardless of an item’s own value. Ratio estimation instead projects the sample’s ratio of audited value to book value onto the population’s book total, and is the more precise choice whenever errors tend to scale with the size of the item rather than remaining constant in dollar terms.

    A scenario worth recognizing

    Suppose an accounts receivable confirmation exercise draws a monetary unit sample of sixty invoices from a receivable population with a book total of eight million four hundred thousand dollars, out of two thousand one hundred outstanding invoices. Of the sixty invoices selected, fifty-six confirm exactly with the customer, and four confirm at a lower amount than recorded, reflecting short payments not yet applied in the ledger, for shortfalls of $150.00, $220.00, $95.00, and $310.00.

  • With the sixty sampled items entered as a dataset carrying a Book Value Column and an Audited Value Column, open Variables Sampling from the sidebar and switch to the Evaluate Sample Results tab.
  • Set Book Value Column and Audited Value Column to the two columns holding the recorded and confirmed amounts.
  • Set Population Size to 2100 and Population Book Total to 8400000, and leave Confidence Level at 95.
  • Under Estimation Method, select Difference, since the four shortfalls found are closer to a constant dollar amount than a constant proportion of invoice size.
  • Click Evaluate Sample.

    • Whichever method is chosen, the evaluation returns a point estimate of the population’s true value, the implied projected misstatement, and a precision figure, computed at the chosen confidence level and adjusted by the same finite population correction used in sample size planning, that expresses the range within which the population’s true value is expected to fall. In the run above, that precision is $27,787.90 on a projected misstatement of negative $27,125.00, giving a standard error of $14,177.50 from a sample of sixty items drawn against a population of two thousand one hundred. If the resulting upper bound of likely misstatement remains comfortably below the engagement’s materiality threshold, as it does here, the population can be accepted as fairly stated; if it does not, the sample has done exactly what it was designed to do, which is to indicate that further work on the population is required before an opinion can be supported.

    Interpreting the Result

    When a sample evaluation projects a misstatement

    1. Benign explanation. A small number of timing differences, such as a payment made shortly before period end that had not yet been recorded when the population was extracted, can account for a modest projected misstatement without indicating any underlying error in the recording process itself.
    2. Error or judgment lapse. A consistent, one-directional difference across most or all of the exceptions in a sample, rather than differences scattered in both directions, suggests a systematic cause, such as a miscalculated rate applied uniformly, rather than isolated mistakes.
    3. What would indicate something more serious. Exceptions concentrated among items associated with a specific customer, region, or approver, combined with a pattern of responses that appear designed to avoid a direct confirmation, warrant an expanded sample and direct inquiry beyond what the statistical projection alone can resolve.

    Part III

    Internal Controls

    Chapter 12

    Segregation of Duties and Access Review

    A control built entirely around a single person’s honesty is not a control. Segregation of duties addresses this by ensuring that no one individual holds two or more incompatible responsibilities within the same process, such as creating a vendor record and also approving payments to that vendor, so that a single person acting alone cannot both cause a transaction and approve it. Access review addresses a related but distinct question: whether the technical permissions granted to a system continue to match the person’s current employment status and role, since a termination or a transfer that is not promptly reflected in system access leaves a door open that no one is actively watching.

    The Working Dataset for This Chapter

    This chapter introduces a third recurring file, user_activity_log.csv, an extract of twenty-one system activity records covering eleven users of Meridian Office Supply Co.’s procurement and payment system over January 2025. Each row records one user performing one action on one date, together with that user’s current employment status and, where applicable, a termination date.

    Running a Segregation of Duties Scan

    Segregation of Duties Analysis is reached by right-clicking any column header and choosing Audit → SOX SoD Analysis..., or from the top menu bar’s Audit → Audit Checks submenu. It opens a dedicated dialog rather than the generic parameter form most audit operations use, since defining a set of toxic combinations benefits from a purpose-built table rather than a single-row parameter list.

  • Right-click any column header in user_activity_log.csv and choose Audit → SOX SoD Analysis....
  • Set User ID Column to user_id and Action/Role Column to action.
  • Under Load Template, select Procure to Pay (P2P). Three toxic combinations populate automatically: Create Vendor paired with Pay Vendor, Create PO paired with Approve PO, and Receive Goods paired with Approve Invoice, each at High severity.
  • Click Scan for Conflicts.

    • Two new columns, sod_conflict_found and sod_conflict_detail, are added to every row belonging to a user who holds both sides of at least one toxic combination, not merely to the specific rows where the conflicting actions themselves appear.     UserConflict Detail
    Elena PetrovaHigh: Create Vendor + Pay Vendor

    Figure 12.3 — Every user in the working file who holds both sides of a Procure to Pay toxic combination. Grace Liu, who holds Create Vendor and Create PO, is not flagged, since that specific pairing is not one of the three rules loaded.

    Toxic Combinations Beyond a Pair

    The optional third column in the conflict table exists for a genuinely three-way toxic combination, where a finding depends on a user holding all three of a set of actions rather than any two. A user who can create a purchase order, approve that same purchase order, and record the goods as received controls an entire acquisition cycle alone, a materially different risk from holding any two of those three capabilities on their own. CaatMaster evaluates this the same way it evaluates a pairwise rule: a user is flagged only if every non-blank action in the row is present in that user’s own action history, so a three-way rule with two of its three conditions met does not produce a partial or watered-down flag.

    Running an Access Review

    SOX Access Review, reached the same way as the SoD scan, by right-clicking any column header and choosing Audit → SOX Access Review..., flags every activity record belonging to a user whose status column currently reads as terminated, inactive, disabled, or suspended, a list of qualifying values that can be edited directly in the dialog.

  • Right-click any column header in user_activity_log.csv and choose Audit → SOX Access Review....
  • Set User Status Column to status.
  • Set Activity Date Column to action_date and Termination Date Column to termination_date. Both are optional; supplying them extends the check to also flag activity dated on or after a recorded termination date, regardless of what the status column currently shows.
  • Click Run Access Review.

    • Run against the working file, this flags all four activity records belonging to the two users whose status column currently reads Terminated: three records for Wendy Chu and one for Robert Lin. This result rewards a closer look rather than a single glance. Every one of a currently terminated user’s logged actions is flagged, not only the ones recorded after that user’s termination date, because the fact that a user is now terminated is itself a reason to confirm that everything they did while employed was legitimate. The termination date supplied alongside the status becomes useful precisely for telling these flagged records apart from one another: Robert Lin’s single flagged record is dated December 10, 2024, ten days before his December 20, 2024 termination date, while one of Wendy Chu’s three flagged records is dated January 22, 2025, seven days after her January 15, 2025 termination date. The flag column alone cannot make this distinction; the reviewer has to look at the dates.

    A scenario worth recognizing

    Suppose an internal audit team runs an access review against a full year of ERP activity for a company with four hundred active users and reviews every flagged record by status alone, without cross-referencing the termination date column also present in the extract. The review concludes that eighteen terminated employees generated activity while marked terminated in the system, and reports this as eighteen access control failures of roughly equal severity.

    A closer reading of the termination dates shows that fifteen of the eighteen are timing artifacts: the status field was updated on the employee’s last physical day in the office, while their final approved expense reports and timesheet submissions, entirely legitimate, posted to the system over the following one to two weeks through a normal payroll cutoff process. The remaining three, however, show system activity dated three to six weeks after both the status change and the termination date, well past any plausible administrative lag, and involve one user who continued approving purchase orders a full month after departure. Treating all eighteen as equally severe would have buried the three findings that actually matter inside fifteen that do not.

    Interpreting the Result

    When a user is flagged for a toxic combination or post-termination activity

    1. Benign explanation. A small company or a backup-coverage arrangement during a colleague’s absence can require one person to temporarily hold two normally separated responsibilities, with a compensating control, such as a supervisor’s independent review, standing in for the segregation that role design alone does not provide.
    2. Error or judgment lapse. A termination processed in the human resources system without a corresponding, timely removal of system access is usually an administrative gap between two systems that do not automatically synchronize, rather than a deliberate decision to leave access open.
    3. What would indicate something more serious. Continued, substantive activity, such as approving payments rather than a single delayed administrative transaction, well beyond any plausible processing lag after a termination date, combined with no compensating review of that activity by anyone else, warrants immediate escalation rather than inclusion in a routine finding.

    Chapter 13

    Mapping Findings to COSO

    A list of findings, however well supported each one is individually, does not by itself tell an audit committee where an organization’s control environment is weakest. The COSO Internal Control Framework, published by the Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission and the most widely referenced control framework in financial statement auditing, organizes internal control into five components: Control Environment, the tone and structure an organization sets for control consciousness; Risk Assessment, the process of identifying and analyzing risks to objectives; Control Activities, the specific policies and procedures that address those risks; Information and Communication, the systems that ensure relevant information reaches the people who need it; and Monitoring Activities, the ongoing and separate evaluations that confirm the other four components continue to function. Mapping a set of findings onto these five components turns a flat list into a picture of where control weakness actually concentrates.

    Two Ways CaatMaster Builds a Heatmap

    CaatMaster offers two paths to a COSO heatmap, suited to two different situations. Where individual findings have already been produced elsewhere in the application, each carrying its own COSO component and severity, as every rule in the deterministic rule libraries covered in the next chapter already does, the heatmap can be built directly from that list of findings, with no further mapping step required. Where a reviewer instead starts from a general risk register or a list of process areas that have not yet been tagged with a COSO component, the COSO Risk Heatmap operation described below provides the mapping step itself, as part of running the operation.

    Running a COSO Risk Heatmap

    COSO Risk Heatmap, reached by right-clicking any column header and choosing Audit → COSO Risk Heatmap..., takes a category column, such as a process area or business unit, and a numeric risk score column, and produces a summary table with one row per COSO component, aggregating the average and maximum risk score and the number of underlying issues mapped to each. This chapter’s working example uses a fourth file, process_risk_register.csv, an eight-row risk register listing distinct process areas across Meridian Office Supply Co. together with a risk score from zero to ten previously assigned during a risk assessment workshop.

  • With process_risk_register.csv open, right-click any column header and choose Audit → COSO Risk Heatmap....
  • Set Category/Process Column to process_area and Risk Score Column to risk_score.
  • Click Load Unique Categories. One row appears per distinct process area, each with its own COSO Component selector, defaulted to Control Environment.
  • Set each row’s COSO Component: IT User Access Provisioning and Accounts Payable Authorization to Control Activities; Vendor Master Maintenance to Control Environment; Sales Order Credit Checks and Board Risk Committee Reporting to Risk Assessment; Journal Entry Review and Physical Inventory Counts to Monitoring; Whistleblower Hotline Monitoring to Info & Comm.
  • Click Generate Heatmap Data.
    • COSO ComponentAvg Risk ScoreMax Risk ScoreIssue Count
    Control Activities7.758.02
    Control Environment7.07.01
    Monitoring Activities5.756.02
    Risk Assessment4.04.52
    Information & Communication3.03.01

    Figure 13.2 — The resulting heatmap, sorted by average risk score. Control Activities carries both the highest average and the highest single risk score in this register, driven by the Accounts Payable Authorization and IT User Access Provisioning process areas.

    Every figure in this table traces back to a risk score a reviewer assigned directly to a named process area during the underlying risk assessment; CaatMaster contributes the aggregation and the mapping, not the underlying judgment about how risky any one process area actually is. A component score is only as reliable as the risk scores and the category-to-component mapping supplied to produce it, and both belong in the workpaper alongside the resulting heatmap.

    A scenario worth recognizing

    Suppose a controls self-assessment across a larger organization’s forty process areas produces a heatmap showing Control Activities and Monitoring Activities both scoring above seven on a ten-point scale, while Control Environment scores below three. Read in isolation, the low Control Environment score might appear to be the strongest result on the page. Read against COSO’s own framework, in which Control Environment is described as the foundation the other four components depend on, a low score there deserves more attention, not less, since a weak tone at the top can eventually undermine control activities and monitoring that currently test as strong, even though today’s heatmap does not yet show any resulting deterioration in those components.

    Interpreting the Result

    When one COSO component scores markedly higher than the others

    1. Benign explanation. A single component can score high simply because more findings have been actively looked for and documented there, such as a recently completed IT general controls review, rather than because that component is genuinely weaker than areas that have not yet been reviewed as closely.
    2. Error or judgment lapse. A category-to-component mapping applied inconsistently, such as one reviewer routing access-related findings to Control Activities and another routing similar findings to Information and Communication, can distort a heatmap in a way that has nothing to do with the underlying risk.
    3. What would indicate something more serious. A Control Environment score that is low not because it has been under-reviewed but because specific, documented findings, such as an unresolved whistleblower complaint or a compromised reporting line, support it, warrants escalation to the audit committee regardless of how the other four components currently score.

    Chapter 14

    Deterministic Rule Libraries

    Chapter 4 described a governing rule for CaatMaster’s AI-assisted features: a language model may be asked to translate a policy written in prose into a structured, checkable condition, but the condition itself is always evaluated against the complete dataset using ordinary, deterministic code. The deterministic rule libraries covered in this chapter apply the second half of that pattern without needing the first half at all. Each rule ships with its checkable condition already written by hand, against logical field names such as amount or approver, so that running it requires only mapping those logical names to the actual column names in a specific dataset, with no AI provider, no API cost, and no translation step of any kind.

    The Libraries CaatMaster Ships With

    Three libraries are included as of this writing, spanning eight individual rules in total. SOX — Accounts Payable & Procurement Controls contains three rules: Payment Without Approval on File, which flags any payment at or above a configurable threshold with no approver recorded; Duplicate Vendor Payment, which flags any repeated combination of vendor, amount, and reference number; and Payment Just Below Approval Threshold, which flags payments falling in the ten percent band immediately under the approval threshold, a deterministic counterpart to the threshold-avoidance pattern introduced through Benford’s Law in Chapter 8. COSO — Expense & Travel Control Activities contains three parallel rules aimed at expense reimbursement: Expense Without Receipt Reference, Expense Over Policy Limit, and Duplicate Expense Claim. Period-End Journal Entry Risk contains two rules aimed at the manual journal entries examined in a typical ISA 240 fraud-risk procedure: Large Manual/Topside Journal Entry and Journal Entry Missing Description.

    Every rule in every library carries its own citation, its COSO component, a default severity, and a plain-language description and recommendation, so that a finding produced by a rule library arrives already written in the vocabulary of a workpaper rather than as a bare true-or-false flag.

    Running a Rule Library Check

    Rule libraries are reached from the top menu bar through Reports → LLM Analysis..., despite that menu label, which names the dialog’s original purpose rather than everything it now does; the Rule Detection tab of the dialog this opens runs entirely without AI. This chapter revisits the missing-approver finding from Chapter 6 and the near-threshold outlier from Chapter 8 and Chapter 10, and shows both are also reachable as a single, named, citable rule.

  • From the top menu bar, choose Reports → LLM Analysis... against the AP Transactions dataset, and open the Rule Detection tab.
  • Select the SOX — Accounts Payable & Procurement Controls library, then choose the Payment Without Approval on File rule. CaatMaster proposes a mapping from the rule’s logical fields to matching columns in the open dataset.
  • Confirm amount maps to amount and approver maps to approver, and set reference to invoice_id.
  • Lower the Approval threshold ($) parameter from its default of 10000 to 300, since this working file’s amounts are far smaller than a typical company-wide approval limit.
  • Click Run Rules.

    • The rule flags the same five records Chapter 6’s no-nulls check on the approver column found, for a combined exposed amount of $4,248.40, because both tests are, underneath their different names, asking the same question of the same data. Where the rule library adds real value over the completeness check alone is in what it hands back: not just a fail count, but a named finding, SOX 404 — Control Activities (Authorization), a COSO component, Control Activities, a severity, high, and a ready-made recommendation to obtain evidence of approval or correct the workflow, none of which a generic completeness check produces on its own.

    Running the same library’s Payment Just Below Approval Threshold rule at its default $10,000 threshold against the same working file flags exactly one record, invoice 20010, Cascade IT Solutions, $9,900.00, the same invoice already identified as a statistical outlier in Chapter 10. A single population examined through three different techniques in this book, an outlier test, a Benford digit test, and now a named compliance rule, converges on the same transaction, which is a considerably stronger basis for inquiry than any one of the three findings would be alone.

    A scenario worth recognizing

    Suppose a compliance team maintains its authorization policy as a two-page written document, reviewed and re-approved annually by internal audit, stating that payments of ten thousand dollars or more require a named approver on file. Rather than re-reading that document each quarter and manually querying the payment ledger, the team maps the Payment Without Approval on File rule once, at the start of the year, to the general ledger extract’s actual column names, and re-runs it against each new quarterly extract without any further translation step. When the policy is revised mid-year to lower the threshold to seven thousand five hundred dollars, updating the check requires changing one number in the rule’s threshold parameter, not rewriting a query or re-explaining the policy to anyone.

    Interpreting the Result

    When a rule library flags a population of transactions

    1. Benign explanation. A missing approver field can reflect a control that is genuinely performed outside the system under test, such as a paper sign-off retained in a physical file, rather than a control that was skipped entirely.
    2. Error or judgment lapse. A threshold rule calibrated to a company-wide policy, applied without adjustment to a single small department or a small working file, as this chapter’s own example demonstrates, can flag a rate of exceptions that looks alarming purely because the threshold does not match the scale of the population being tested.
    3. What would indicate something more serious. The same transaction surfacing under more than one independent rule or technique, as invoice 20010 does across this book’s outlier, Benford, and rule-library chapters, is a materially stronger signal than any single flag on its own and warrants priority follow-up.

    Part IV

    IFRS Assertions

    Chapter 15

    Revenue Recognition (IFRS 15)

    Revenue recognition is judgment-heavy in a way that few other line items are. IFRS 15 requires revenue to be recognized as an entity satisfies a performance obligation, not on any single, universally observable event, which leaves genuine room for a contract’s margin or its recognition timing to be managed toward a target rather than derived purely from the underlying economics. This chapter covers two deterministic techniques CaatMaster applies to a population of contracts: a control-chart test for a sustained shift in a contract’s margin over time, and a straightforward comparison between the date revenue was recognized and the date the underlying performance obligation was actually satisfied.

    The working file for this chapter, contract_revenue_schedule.csv, holds fourteen rows: three contracts, each reporting revenue and cost across four to six monthly periods, together with a recognition date and a delivery date for every period.

    Every IFRS and IAS operation in this part of the book, including the two covered in this chapter, is reachable two ways: by right-clicking any column header and choosing Financial, the path every walkthrough below uses, or from the top menu bar’s Financial menu, added once early beta feedback flagged that a reviewer had no way to discover these operations without first knowing to right-click a column header. Both paths open the identical dialog and compute identically; neither is more complete than the other.

    Detecting a Margin Shift with CUSUM

    A contract whose margin holds steady for several periods and then moves sharply is a pattern worth understanding, since a sudden shift is more consistent with a change in how costs are being allocated between periods than with a genuine change in the underlying economics of the work. CaatMaster tests for this using a CUSUM, or cumulative sum, control chart, a technique long used in manufacturing quality control to detect a change in a process level. The test accumulates each period’s deviation from the contract’s own baseline margin, allowing a small amount of normal noise, the slack parameter k, before that deviation starts counting, and signals a shift once the accumulated deviation crosses a threshold, h, expressed as a multiple of the margin’s own scale. Both k and h scale automatically with the contract’s own margin volatility, so the same default multipliers apply sensibly whether a contract’s margin normally moves by half a percentage point or by ten.

    The baseline itself is worth a direct word, because an earlier version of this check used the plain mean and standard deviation of the whole margin history to set that baseline, and that choice had a real, verified weakness: this is a retrospective scan of a complete history, not a monitoring chart with a separately established, known-good reference period, so the shift being searched for is necessarily included in the very data used to decide what normal looks like. A single sharp collapse can pull the mean toward it and inflate the standard deviation enough that the collapse no longer clears a multiple of its own inflated denominator, so a genuine shift could go undetected precisely because it was large enough to distort the baseline meant to catch it. CaatMaster now estimates that baseline using the median and the interquartile range instead, both of which stay put unless a shift affects a genuinely large share of the population, which resolved the failure directly: a real six-period contract history, five months of stable margin followed by one sharp collapse, went from undetected at the default threshold to correctly flagged, with no false positive introduced against a longer, evenly-split synthetic history used elsewhere to test this same function.

  • With contract_revenue_schedule.csv open, right-click any column header and choose Financial → IFRS 15 Margin Shift Detection (CUSUM)....
  • Set Revenue Column to revenue, Cost Column to cost, Period Date Column to recognition_date, and Contract/Group Column to contract_id, so the CUSUM baseline is computed independently for each contract rather than across the whole population.
  • Leave Slack (k) and Threshold (h) at their defaults of 0.50 and 4.00.
  • Click Detect Margin Shifts.

    • Contract CT-1001 runs at a stable margin near forty percent for five months, then drops to fifteen percent in the sixth. At the default threshold, this is now flagged correctly, and neither of the other two contracts, whose margins hold genuinely steady throughout, produces a false positive.

    Checking Revenue Timing Against Delivery

    Revenue Timing Gap is reached the same way, through Financial → IFRS 15 Revenue Timing Gap..., and answers a narrower, more mechanical question: for each row, how many days separate the date revenue was recognized from the date the performance obligation was satisfied. A negative gap means revenue was booked before delivery, a bill-and-hold-style pattern that IFRS 15’s transfer-of-control principle treats as premature recognition unless the specific conditions for recognizing revenue ahead of physical delivery are separately met and documented. Run against this chapter’s working file with Revenue Recognition Date Column set to recognition_date, Delivery/Shipment Date Column set to delivery_date, and the allowed buffer left at its default of zero days, the check flags exactly one row: CT-1003’s March period, recognized twelve days before the goods were actually delivered.

    A scenario worth recognizing

    Suppose a technology reseller runs both checks together across several hundred active contracts at quarter end. The CUSUM test flags four contracts with a sustained margin shift; the timing-gap test flags eleven contracts with revenue recognized ahead of delivery. Two contracts appear on both lists. For those two, the margin shift traces directly to revenue being pulled forward into the current quarter from a shipment that had not yet gone out, inflating the current period’s recognized margin relative to a true, delivery-matched calculation. The other contracts on each list turn out to have independent, unrelated explanations, an unusually large parts cost on one CUSUM-flagged contract and a routine same-week shipping delay on several timing-gap-flagged ones, but the two contracts flagged by both tests together receive priority follow-up precisely because two independent techniques converged on the same population.

    Interpreting the Result

    When a contract is flagged by either test

    1. Benign explanation. A genuine change in a contract’s scope, such as a renegotiated rate for a new phase of work, can produce a real, legitimate step change in margin that a control chart, which has no knowledge of contract terms, cannot distinguish from cost-shifting on its own.
    2. Error or judgment lapse. A shipping or paperwork delay that causes revenue to be booked slightly ahead of a delivery confirmation being logged in the system is a timing and process issue, not typically an attempt to misstate results, particularly where the gap is small and consistent across many unrelated contracts.
    3. What would indicate something more serious. A margin shift concentrated in the final period of a reporting quarter, affecting several contracts under the same account manager, combined with a timing gap that grows specifically at quarter end rather than remaining constant throughout the year, is a pattern consistent with deliberate period-end management rather than routine operational noise.

    Chapter 16

    Expected Credit Losses (IFRS 9)

    IFRS 9 replaced the older incurred-loss model for financial asset impairment with an expected credit loss model, requiring an entity to recognize a loss allowance based on forward-looking expectations rather than waiting for objective evidence that a loss has already happened. This forward-looking requirement is implemented through a three-stage classification, Stage 1 for performing assets, Stage 2 for assets that have experienced a significant increase in credit risk since origination, and Stage 3 for assets that are credit-impaired, with the expected credit loss calculation growing more conservative at each stage. This chapter covers CaatMaster’s two IFRS 9 techniques: staging a loan population and calculating its expected credit loss, and recalculating that loss as a probability-weighted average across macroeconomic scenarios rather than a single point estimate.

    The working file, loan_portfolio.csv, holds ten loans, each carrying an exposure balance, a days-past-due figure, a current and an at-origination probability of default, a loss given default assumption, probability of default estimates under base, upside, and downside macroeconomic scenarios, and management’s own booked expected credit loss for comparison.

    Staging a Portfolio and Calculating ECL

    IFRS 9 Staging, reached by right-clicking any column header and choosing Financial → IFRS 9 Staging..., classifies each loan by days past due, using the standard convention of thirty days as the boundary into Stage 2 and ninety days as the boundary into Stage 3, both configurable on the dialog’s second tab. Where exposure, probability of default, and loss given default are all mapped, it additionally calculates an expected credit loss for every row as the direct product of the three, the standard EAD times PD times LGD formula.

  • Right-click any column header in loan_portfolio.csv and choose Financial → IFRS 9 Staging....
  • Confirm Days Past Due (DPD) maps to dpd, Exposure (EAD) to exposure, and Loss Given Default (LGD) to lgd, all detected automatically from the column names.
  • Set Prob. Default (PD) to pd_current.
  • Under SICR Trigger by PD Deterioration, set Current PD to pd_current and PD at Origination to pd_origination. On the Thresholds tab, set the SICR PD Multiplier to 3.00x: a loan whose current probability of default has risen to three times its probability at origination is escalated to Stage 2 even if it remains fully current on its payments.
  • Click Run Staging Analysis.
    • LoanDPDStageStatusECL
    L00602Underperforming2,025.00
    L002452Underperforming8,000.00
    L010352Underperforming14,630.00
    L0041003Non-Performing23,100.00
    L008953Non-Performing12,000.00

    Figure 16.2 — Every loan staged above Stage 1. L006 is the case the SICR trigger exists for: zero days past due, current on every payment, but escalated to Stage 2 because its probability of default has risen to five times what it was at origination.

    Recalculating ECL Across Scenarios

    IFRS 9 Scenario-Weighted ECL, reached through Financial → IFRS 9 Scenario-Weighted ECL..., recalculates expected credit loss as a probability-weighted average across base, upside, and downside macroeconomic scenarios, rather than management’s single point-estimate probability of default, and, where management’s own booked figure is mapped, flags any loan where the two differ by more than a chosen threshold. Run against loan_portfolio.csv with the default scenario weights of fifty percent base, twenty-five percent upside, and twenty-five percent downside, and a twenty percent variance threshold, one loan is flagged: L008, whose recalculated scenario-weighted expected credit loss of $12,000.00 exceeds management’s booked $7,000.00 by 41.67 percent, a full-population, deterministic recalculation, not a simulation with a different random result on every run.

    A scenario worth recognizing

    Suppose a bank’s allowance committee sets scenario weights of forty percent base, twenty percent upside, and forty percent downside ahead of an anticipated economic slowdown, a heavier downside weighting than the fifty-twenty-five-twenty-five split used in the walkthrough above. Recalculating the same loan population under the heavier downside weighting raises the scenario-weighted expected credit loss on every loan with a meaningfully worse downside probability of default than its base case, and a loan that passed the twenty percent variance check under the original weights can fail it under the revised ones. Neither weighting is more correct in the abstract; the choice belongs to the allowance committee’s own judgment about the economic outlook, and CaatMaster’s role is to make that judgment’s consequences visible across the whole portfolio at once, rather than to make the judgment itself.

    Interpreting the Result

    When a loan is escalated to Stage 2 or 3, or its ECL varies materially from management’s figure

    1. Benign explanation. A loan escalated purely by the SICR trigger, while remaining current on every payment, may reflect a genuine, temporary deterioration in a single credit factor, such as a covenant metric, that the borrower has already begun correcting, rather than a change that ultimately proves permanent.
    2. Error or judgment lapse. A material ECL variance can trace to a stale probability of default that was not refreshed at the reporting date, an input error rather than a deliberate understatement.
    3. What would indicate something more serious. A pattern of management’s booked ECL consistently landing below the recalculated figure across many loans, rather than scattered in both directions, together with no documented, loan-specific reason for each variance, warrants inquiry into whether the allowance process itself is biased toward understatement.

    Chapter 17

    Leases (IFRS 16)

    IFRS 16 requires a lessee to recognize almost every lease on the balance sheet, as a lease liability equal to the present value of remaining lease payments and a corresponding right-of-use asset. The single input with the most leverage over the size of that recorded liability, and the one most exposed to management judgment, is the discount rate applied to those future payments, the lessee’s incremental borrowing rate. A higher discount rate produces a lower present value and therefore a smaller recorded liability from the same stream of payments, which means an aggressively high incremental borrowing rate is a direct, quantifiable way a lease obligation can be understated without changing a single contractual payment term.

    The working file, lease_schedule.csv, holds six leases, each with a periodic payment amount, the number of remaining payment periods, management’s selected incremental borrowing rate, a benchmark rate for comparison, and, for two of the leases, initial direct costs and lease incentives that adjust the right-of-use asset without affecting the liability itself.

    Running the Lease Liability and IBR Check

    IFRS 16 Lease Liability & IBR Check, reached by right-clicking any column header and choosing Financial → IFRS 16 Lease Liability & IBR Check..., calculates each lease’s liability as the present value of an ordinary annuity of its remaining payments, discounted at management’s incremental borrowing rate. Where a benchmark rate is also supplied, typically a risk-free rate plus an appropriate credit spread that the reviewer determines independently, CaatMaster does not build or assume any credit-spread model itself, it recalculates the same liability using that benchmark rate and flags any lease whose management-selected rate deviates from the benchmark by more than a chosen number of basis points.

  • Right-click any column header in lease_schedule.csv and choose Financial → IFRS 16 Lease Liability & IBR Check....
  • Set Periodic Payment Amount to payment, Remaining Number of Periods to periods, and Management’s IBR to management_ibr.
  • Set Benchmark IBR to benchmark_ibr, Initial Direct Costs to initial_direct_costs, and Lease Incentives to lease_incentives.
  • Leave the flag threshold at its default of 50.00 bps.
  • Click Calculate Lease Liability.
    • LeaseMgmt IBRBenchmark IBRDeviation (bps)LiabilityUnderstatement

    Figure 17.2 — The single lease flagged. Management’s 0.90 percent monthly rate, against a 0.35 percent benchmark, understates this lease’s recorded liability by $10,033.57 relative to what the benchmark rate would have produced. The other five leases each deviate by two basis points or less and are not flagged.

    A scenario worth recognizing

    Suppose a logistics company leases its delivery fleet under a series of short-term vehicle leases and applies a single, company-wide incremental borrowing rate to every lease on its books, regardless of the underlying asset’s type or the lease term’s length. A benchmark rate built specifically for vehicle-class assets, reflecting their shorter useful life and the fact that a vehicle lease is typically well secured by the vehicle itself, comes in meaningfully lower than the company-wide rate applied to real estate and equipment leases alike. Every vehicle lease in the portfolio is flagged, not because any single lease was deliberately mismeasured, but because a rate genuinely appropriate for a ten-year office lease was applied uniformly to three-year vehicle leases with a very different risk profile.

    Interpreting the Result

    When a lease’s incremental borrowing rate deviates from the benchmark

    1. Benign explanation. A genuinely higher incremental borrowing rate can be appropriate for an asset class or a counterparty with real, documented credit risk that the general benchmark rate does not reflect.
    2. Error or judgment lapse. A single company-wide rate applied without adjustment for asset class or lease term, as in the scenario above, produces a mechanical rather than deliberate deviation, correctable by refining how the rate is set rather than by any individual lease.
    3. What would indicate something more serious. A pattern of high IBRs concentrated specifically among the largest leases, or those closest to a debt covenant threshold that a smaller recorded lease liability would help preserve, warrants a closer look at how each rate was actually determined.

    Chapter 18

    Impairment (IAS 36)

    IAS 36 requires an asset, or a cash-generating unit, the smallest identifiable group of assets that generates independent cash inflows, to be tested for impairment whenever there is an indication its carrying value may not be recoverable, and impaired down to its recoverable amount when it is not. Where recoverable amount is estimated as a value in use, a discounted cash flow model, the forecast itself is built from management’s own assumptions, including a terminal growth rate applied to cash flows beyond the explicit forecast period, an assumption with no external market price to check it against directly. CaatMaster addresses this by running the discounted cash flow model in reverse: rather than taking a terminal growth assumption as an input and calculating whether the resulting valuation supports the carrying value, it takes the carrying value as fixed and solves for the exact terminal growth rate that value implies.

    The working file, cgu_impairment_test.csv, holds four cash-generating units, each with a carrying value, a discount rate, and five years of explicit-period cash flow forecasts.

    Running the Reverse-DCF Test

    IAS 36 Implied Growth Rate (Reverse DCF), reached by right-clicking any column header and choosing Financial → IAS 36 Implied Growth Rate (Reverse DCF)..., solves for the terminal growth rate g that makes the present value of the explicit-period cash flows plus a Gordon-growth terminal value exactly equal the carrying value, using numerical root-finding rather than a closed-form formula, since the equation is not linear in g once more than one explicit cash flow period is involved. Where no valid growth rate exists in a plausible range, typically because the explicit cash flows alone already exceed the carrying value even without any terminal growth at all, CaatMaster reports a missing value rather than forcing a number, consistent with the standing rule described in Chapter 4 against ever fabricating a figure that cannot actually be computed.

  • Right-click any column header in cgu_impairment_test.csv and choose Financial → IAS 36 Implied Growth Rate (Reverse DCF)....
  • Set Carrying Value Column to carrying_value and Discount Rate Column to discount_rate.
  • Under Explicit-Period Cash Flow Columns, click + Add Year four times to reach five rows, and set them in order to cf_y1 through cf_y5.
  • Under Growth Benchmark, select Use a single benchmark value and enter 0.0250, a long-run GDP-growth-style benchmark applied to every row. Leave the flag threshold at its default of 2.00 pp.
  • Click Solve Implied Growth Rate.

    CGU-Retail-South3,200,000−4.70%−7.20 ppNo

    Figure 18.2 — CGU-Retail-North requires a 4.71 percent perpetual growth rate to support its carrying value, 2.21 percentage points above the 2.5 percent benchmark, and is flagged. The other three CGUs imply negative growth requirements, meaning their explicit forecast cash flows alone comfortably support the carrying value without needing any terminal growth assumption at all, let alone an aggressive one.

    A scenario worth recognizing

    Suppose a retail chain’s largest cash-generating unit implies a required terminal growth rate of six percent against a benchmark of two and a half percent, a three-and-a-half-point gap comfortably past the flag threshold. Management’s support for the underlying carrying value cites a store-remodeling program expected to lift same-store sales meaningfully above the broader market for several years. A six percent perpetual growth rate, sustained forever rather than for the two or three years a remodel’s effect might reasonably be expected to last, is a materially different claim than a temporary lift, and the reviewer’s question becomes specifically whether management’s five-year explicit forecast already captures the remodel’s expected benefit, in which case a lower, more defensible terminal growth rate should be sufficient, or whether the remodel’s benefit has been pushed into the unobservable terminal period precisely because it is easier to support a growth assumption there than a specific, checkable forecast figure.

    Interpreting the Result

    When a CGU’s implied growth rate exceeds the benchmark

    1. Benign explanation. A CGU operating in a genuinely higher-growth market or geography than the general benchmark reflects can legitimately support an above-benchmark terminal growth rate, provided that market’s own growth characteristics are documented.
    2. Error or judgment lapse. An overly optimistic explicit-period forecast, carried through mechanically into the terminal growth solve, can produce a high implied rate that traces back to the forecast itself rather than to any terminal-period assumption being separately aggressive.
    3. What would indicate something more serious. An implied growth rate that has increased year over year specifically to avoid recognizing an impairment that a more conservative, consistent growth assumption would trigger, without any corresponding change in the CGU’s actual business prospects, warrants direct challenge of the underlying forecast.

    Chapter 19

    Provisions and Inventory (IAS 37, IAS 2)

    This chapter covers two shorter, more mechanical tests, paired together because each addresses a balance that depends on management’s own estimate of a future outcome, a provision for a probable future obligation under IAS 37 and the net realizable value of inventory under IAS 2, and each is more useful as a triage tool that narrows a large population down to a short list worth a closer look than as a standalone conclusion.

    Provision Trend Breaks

    A provision balance that moves sharply from one year to the next deserves a closer look regardless of the direction of the move, though a large decrease is generally the higher-risk case, since it can reflect an obligation being released without a corresponding event that actually justifies releasing it, sometimes called income smoothing through the provisions balance. IAS 37 Provision Trend Break, reached by right-clicking any column header and choosing Financial → IAS 37 Provision Trend Break..., flags any provision category whose year-over-year balance changed by more than a chosen percentage, and, where a settlement or legal-claim indicator has already been joined onto the same population, distinguishes a flagged decrease that lines up with a recorded settlement from one that does not.

  • Right-click any column header in provisions_register.csv and choose Financial → IAS 37 Provision Trend Break....
  • Set Prior Year Balance Column to prior_year, Current Year Balance Column to current_year, and Settlement/Claim Flag Column to settlement_flag.
  • Leave the flag threshold at its default of 30.00%.
  • Click Check Provision Trend.

    • Two of the five provision categories in the working file move by more than thirty percent. Legal Claims Provision drops sixty-seven percent year over year, from $1,200,000 to $400,000, but the settlement flag on that row is set, so the decrease, while still flagged as a trend break, is not additionally flagged as unexplained. Environmental Remediation drops sixty-four percent, from $500,000 to $180,000, with no recorded settlement, and is flagged as an unexplained decrease. The distinction the settlement flag draws is exactly the distinction a reviewer would otherwise have to make by hand, row by row, against a separate legal-claims schedule.

    Inventory Net Realizable Value

    IAS 2 requires inventory to be carried at the lower of cost and net realizable value, its estimated selling price less the estimated costs still required to complete and sell it. IAS 2 Inventory NRV Write-Down, reached through Financial → IAS 2 Inventory NRV Write-Down..., calculates net realizable value for every SKU and flags, with a computed dollar write-down amount, any line where cost exceeds it.

    Run against inventory_valuation.csv with cost mapped to cost, selling price to selling_price, costs to sell to costs_to_sell, and quantity to quantity, two of the five SKUs require a write-down: Legacy Printer Cartridges, carried at $18.50 against a net realizable value of $13.00, a $5.50 per-unit excess across five hundred units for a $2,750.00 total write-down, and Discontinued Monitor Stands, carried at $32.00 against a net realizable value of $17.00, a $15.00 per-unit excess across one hundred fifty units for a $2,250.00 write-down. The combined write-down across the population is $5,000.00.

    A scenario worth recognizing

    Suppose a distributor runs both checks together ahead of year end and finds that its largest flagged NRV write-down, on a discontinued product line, coincides with a provision category for inventory obsolescence that dropped sharply in the same period with no recorded settlement. The two findings, examined separately, each look like an isolated estimate that moved. Examined together, they suggest the same underlying fact, that a discontinued line has lost value, is being recognized inconsistently: the specific inventory items are being written down toward realistic values, while the general obsolescence provision meant to anticipate exactly this kind of loss is simultaneously being released, which has the net effect of understating the period’s combined impact from the same underlying cause.

    Interpreting the Result

    When a provision breaks trend or an inventory line requires a write-down

    1. Benign explanation. A provision decrease can reflect a genuine, favorable resolution, such as a claim withdrawn or a warranty period expiring without incident, and an inventory write-down can reflect an honestly recognized, ordinary consequence of a product reaching the end of its life cycle.
    2. Error or judgment lapse. A provision release recorded before the underlying uncertainty was actually resolved, based on an optimistic assessment rather than a confirmed outcome, is a premature judgment call rather than a deliberate misstatement.
    3. What would indicate something more serious. A provision release and an inventory write-down affecting the same underlying cause, recognized in a way that understates their combined effect on the period, as in the scenario above, or a pattern of unexplained provision decreases concentrated in periods immediately before a debt covenant test, warrants a coordinated review of both balances together rather than each in isolation.

    Chapter 20

    Tax and Currency (IAS 12, IAS 21)

    This final chapter of Part IV covers two tests unrelated in subject matter but similar in shape: each takes a balance built from an estimate or a rate a preparer selected, and checks it against an independently determinable benchmark, a recoverability test for a deferred tax asset under IAS 12, and a rate-consistency check for foreign-currency transactions under IAS 21.

    Deferred Tax Asset Recoverability

    A deferred tax asset, commonly arising from a tax loss carried forward, is only recognized to the extent future taxable profit is probable within the window available to use it. IAS 12 DTA Recoverability Check, reached by right-clicking any column header and choosing Financial → IAS 12 DTA Recoverability Check..., inverts this test: rather than asking whether a forecast supports the recognized balance, it solves the plain algebra for the average annual taxable profit the balance itself requires, dta_balance divided by the product of the tax rate and the number of years available to use it, since a deferred tax asset is not discounted under IAS 12, unlike a lease liability or an impairment cash flow model, so no root-finding is needed here. It then compares that required figure to a benchmark profit, typically the entity’s own historical average.

  • Right-click any column header in deferred_tax_register.csv and choose Financial → IAS 12 DTA Recoverability Check....
  • Confirm DTA Balance Column, Tax Rate Column, and Utilization Years Remaining Column map to dta_balance, tax_rate, and utilization_years, all detected automatically.
  • Under Benchmark Taxable Profit, select Use a per-row benchmark column and set it to benchmark_profit.
  • Leave the flag threshold at its default of 20.00%.
  • Click Check DTA Recoverability.
