    Foreign Currency Rate Consistency

    IAS 21 FX Rate Consistency Check, reached through Financial → IAS 21 FX Rate Consistency Check..., compares the exchange rate actually used to record each foreign-currency transaction against a benchmark rate, typically the published spot or closing rate for that date and currency pair, already joined onto the population beforehand. Run against fx_transactions.csv with booked_rate, benchmark_rate, and local_amount mapped and the tolerance left at its default of 1.0%, one transaction is flagged: FX-2002, a GBP/USD payment booked at 1.2650 against a benchmark of 1.2400, a 2.02 percent deviation, understating the transaction’s recorded USD value by $2,125.00 relative to what the benchmark rate would have produced.

    A scenario worth recognizing

    Suppose a multinational’s treasury function books most foreign-currency receipts using a rate pulled automatically from its banking platform at the moment of settlement, but one regional office continues to key in rates manually from a printed daily rate sheet distributed each morning. Every transaction from that regional office shows a small, consistent deviation from the benchmark rate, not because any individual transaction was mishandled, but because a rate fixed at the start of the day drifts slightly from the actual settlement-time rate by the time a transaction clears in the afternoon. The pattern across many small, similarly sized deviations from one specific office is a process finding about that office’s rate source, not a series of unrelated individual errors.

    Interpreting the Result

    When a DTA’s required profit exceeds its benchmark, or an FX rate deviates from the benchmark

    1. Benign explanation. A newly established subsidiary, like Subsidiary C above, may genuinely lack a meaningful historical profit benchmark, and a forward-looking business plan, rather than thin historical results, may be the more appropriate support for its recognized deferred tax asset.
    2. Error or judgment lapse. An FX rate deviation traced to a single office’s outdated rate source, as in the scenario above, is a process gap correctable by standardizing the rate source, not a series of individually mishandled transactions.
    3. What would indicate something more serious. A deferred tax asset whose required profit has grown for several consecutive periods without a corresponding, documented improvement in the underlying business’s actual prospects, or FX rate deviations that consistently favor a more advantageous reported result rather than scattering randomly around the benchmark, both warrant escalation beyond a routine finding.

    Part V

    Source Data

    Chapter 21

    Ratio Analysis Done Right

    Chapter 3 established how a single messy number gets parsed correctly, and Chapter 9 walked through calculating ratios once every figure already sits in a clean, one-row-per-period file with the right column names. Between those two chapters lies the part of the journey most exposed to error in practice: a real financial statement rarely arrives as a clean wide table. It arrives as a trial balance with one row per account, spread across a filing that separates the income statement, the balance sheet, and the cash flow statement into three different exports entirely. This chapter closes that gap, covering how CaatMaster maps an arbitrary account label to the right concept without guessing, and how it recombines statements that were never in the same file to begin with.

    Mapping a Line Item to a Concept, Without Guessing Wrong

    Every automatic concept suggestion in CaatMaster, whether it appears in the Financial Import Wizard from Chapter 3, the Auto-Detect buttons in the Financial Ratios dialog from Chapter 9, or the reshape operation covered below, runs through the same function: a label such as an account name or a column header is checked against a library of patterns, one set per financial concept, and the pattern that matches most specifically wins. Specificity is measured by the length of the matching pattern itself, which is what correctly resolves a label like “Total Current Assets” to current assets rather than the shorter, more generic pattern for total assets, without either pattern needing to be manually ranked against the other. Where two different concepts match a label equally specifically, the function returns nothing rather than picking one arbitrarily, on the reasoning that a silently wrong guess here would feed directly into every ratio calculated from it, and an admitted ambiguity is safer than a confident mistake.

    LabelSuggested Concept
    Total Current Assetscurrent_assets
    Total Assetstotal_assets
    Retained Earningsretained_earnings
    Total Shareholders Equitytotal_equity
    Operating Incomeebit
    Total Revenuerevenue
    Accrued Liabilities(none — left for manual review)

    Figure 21.1 — Real output of CaatMaster’s concept-suggestion function against a set of representative statement labels. Retained Earnings resolves correctly to its own concept rather than being folded into total equity, and Accrued Liabilities, a real account with no corresponding ratio concept, is correctly left unresolved rather than forced into the nearest-sounding option.

    Reshaping a Row-Based Statement

    Reshape Statement to Ratio Inputs, reached by right-clicking any column header and choosing Financial → Reshape Statement to Ratio Inputs..., bridges a statement with accounts as rows into the wide, concept-as-column shape Ratio Analysis needs. Loading the unique account values from a chosen column, it proposes a concept for each one automatically, but only for a row that looks like a subtotal or aggregate line in the first place, such as one containing the word “Total.” A detail-level row, one without that kind of language, defaults to Ignore even where the concept-suggestion function above could resolve it confidently on its own. This is a deliberate, second layer of caution beyond the specificity ranking already described: mapping both an explicit subtotal, such as Total Current Assets, and one of the detail accounts that roll up into it, such as Cash, to concepts at the same time would double-count the same dollars once the two are separately summed into a ratio input, and the dialog would rather leave a real, resolvable row unmapped than risk that silently.

  • Right-click any column header in meridian_trial_balance_q1.csv and choose Financial → Reshape Statement to Ratio Inputs....
  • Set Account/Line Item Column to account, check balance under Value Column(s), and set Period Column to period.
  • Click Load Unique Accounts. Six rows whose label contains “Total” are mapped automatically; six are not.
  • Review the six unmapped rows individually. Set Cash and Cash Equivalents to cash, Interest Expense, Net to interest_expense, Cost of Goods Sold to cogs, Retained Earnings to retained_earnings, and Operating Income to ebit. Leave Accrued Liabilities at Ignore, since no ratio concept corresponds to it.
  • Click Reshape Dataset.

    • The result is a single row for the 2025-Q1 period, carrying eleven mapped concept columns, with Accrued Liabilities correctly absent from the output rather than silently zeroed or guessed into an unrelated concept. That row is now the same shape Chapter 9’s ratio calculation expects, regardless of the fact that it began life as twelve separate account rows rather than a single wide line.

    Combining Statements That Arrive as Separate Files

    The Financial Ratios dialog from Chapter 9 accepts more than one dataset at once specifically for this reason. Its Select Dataset for Each Statement row lets the income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow statement each be pointed at a different open dataset, rather than assuming all three already live in one file; a statement left at Current Dataset simply uses whichever dataset the dialog was opened against.

  • Import income_statement.csv and balance_sheet.csv as two separate datasets, each holding one quarter’s figures for Meridian Office Supply Co.
  • Open Financial Ratios against either dataset.
  • Under Select Dataset for Each Statement, set Income Statement (P&L) to Income Statement and Balance Sheet to Balance Sheet. Leave Cash Flow Statement at Current Dataset, since this example has no separate cash flow file.
  • Map each statement’s columns to concepts as in Chapter 9, then select the ratios to calculate.

    • CaatMaster aligns the two statements by period label before combining them into a single base table, rather than simply pairing up whichever rows happen to occupy the same position in each file, which matters as soon as either statement covers more than one period. Calculated from these two separate files, the resulting ratios, a current ratio of 1.420, a quick ratio of 0.727, a net profit margin of 5.9 percent, and a gross margin of 37.4 percent, match Chapter 9’s fourth-quarter figures exactly, because the two chapters describe the same underlying numbers arriving by two different routes.

    Interpreting the Result

    When a concept is left unmapped, or two statements will not combine

    1. Benign explanation. A genuinely unusual account, or a chart of accounts with its own internal terminology, may simply not correspond to any of CaatMaster’s standard ratio concepts, and Ignore is the correct, final answer for that row rather than a gap to force closed.
    2. Error or judgment lapse. Two statements that fail to combine because their period labels do not match, such as one file using calendar quarters and the other using a fiscal year ending mid-year, points to a labeling inconsistency between two source systems rather than any error in the underlying figures themselves.
    3. What would indicate something more serious. A material concept, such as revenue or total assets, that repeatedly fails to auto-map across many consecutive periods from the same source, forcing a manual override every time, suggests the source system’s own export or chart of accounts has changed in a way that deserves its own investigation, separate from whatever ratio work prompted the reviewer to notice it.

    Chapter 22

    Reading XBRL Directly

    Most regulators now require financial statements to be filed in XBRL, eXtensible Business Reporting Language, or its human-readable variant, inline XBRL, in which the same tags are embedded directly inside an ordinarily formatted HTML filing rather than a separate machine-only document. Every numeric fact in an XBRL filing is tagged against a published taxonomy, US-GAAP or IFRS being the two most common, which means the figures a company reports are, in principle, already machine-readable without anyone needing to copy a number out of a PDF or a spreadsheet export at all. CaatMaster reads both formats directly, using the Arelle library, an open-source XBRL processor with a multi-decade history in regulatory filing software, and maps the tags it finds onto the same standard concepts every other chapter in this part of the book has used.

    Running an Import

    Import XBRL / iXBRL is reached from the top menu bar through File → Import XBRL / iXBRL..., a genuine top-level command rather than something buried in a right-click menu, reflecting how central a filing import is to this workflow. The working file for this chapter, test-multi-period.xml, is a small instance document carrying three Revenue facts: the current year, the prior year, and a current-year figure reported against one specific business segment.

  • From the top menu bar, choose File → Import XBRL / iXBRL....
  • Click Browse... and select the instance document.
  • Click Parse File.

    • The Tagged Elements table lists every distinct element the filing uses, how many individual facts were tagged against it, and CaatMaster’s proposed concept mapping, editable in place exactly like every other concept mapping in this part of the book. The Periods to Include list shows both the current and prior year, each independently selectable for the eventual import. The three facts parsed here include one tagged against a segment dimension rather than the whole entity; left at its default, the Include segment/dimensional facts option keeps that fact out of the resulting dataset, since a segment-level Revenue figure and the consolidated Revenue figure for the same period are not meant to be summed together, and checking that option here would silently produce a period total nearly fifty percent too high, the segment figure counted once as part of the consolidated total and then a second time on its own.

    When a Filing Needs a Taxonomy This Machine Cannot Reach

    An XBRL filing’s own instance document does not contain its taxonomy; it only references one, by a URL that Arelle must resolve, ordinarily by fetching it over the network. On a machine with no internet access, or simply a taxonomy publisher’s server that is temporarily unreachable, this reference cannot resolve, and the import fails outright rather than falling back to a partial or approximate result.

    Manage Taxonomy Packages, reached from the same File menu entry that opens the import dialog, or from the Manage Taxonomy Packages... button inside it, registers a local copy of a taxonomy so every future parse resolves it from disk first, before any network attempt is made at all. A Taxonomy Package is a standard, spec-defined zip file, the same format the SEC and the IFRS Foundation both publish their own official taxonomies in, containing the schema and linkbase files together with a catalog that maps each remote URL a filing might reference back to a local file inside the package.

  • From the Import XBRL / iXBRL dialog, click Manage Taxonomy Packages....
  • Click Add Package... and select the taxonomy package’s zip file.
  • Close the dialog and parse the filing again.

    • With the package registered, reparsing the identical filing that failed above now succeeds, with zero errors and one fact recovered, entirely without a network request ever being attempted, since the catalog inside the package resolves the filing’s schema reference to a local file before Arelle ever considers reaching out over the network. This is not a fallback that activates only after a network attempt times out; the local file is checked first, which is what makes the technique usable on a machine with no internet access at all, not merely one with a slow connection.

    Interpreting the Result

    When a tagged fact will not map to a concept, or a filing will not resolve

    1. Benign explanation. A filer’s own custom extension taxonomy, used for a line item specific to that company’s business, has no standard concept to map to at all, and Ignore, or an unmapped element left out of the final import, is the correct outcome rather than a gap to close.
    2. Error or judgment lapse. A resolution failure on a machine that does have internet access more often traces to a taxonomy publisher’s server being temporarily unreachable than to anything wrong with the filing itself; retrying later, or registering a local package proactively, resolves it without treating the filing as defective.
    3. What would indicate something more serious. A standard concept, such as revenue or total assets, that a filing tags using a heavily customized extension element rather than the standard US-GAAP or IFRS tag every comparable filer uses for the same line item, warrants a direct look at why that specific figure was pulled out of the standard taxonomy.

    Part VI

    AI, Used Responsibly

    Chapter 23

    The Grounded AI Pattern

    Chapter 4 stated the governing rule behind every AI-assisted feature in CaatMaster: a number is never asked of a language model when Polars can compute it exactly. This chapter and the three that follow return to that rule with the detail Chapter 4 deliberately left out, covering how a provider is configured, what CaatMaster actually sends and receives on every call, where that exchange is recorded, and the specific, tested failure modes the translate-then-compute pattern exists to close off.

    Nine Providers, One Interface

    CaatMaster does not build its own language model or commit to a single vendor. It supports nine provider integrations, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, DeepSeek, Hugging Face, Ollama, LlamaCPP, OpenRouter, and a generic custom endpoint for anything compatible with the OpenAI API shape, behind one shared interface. Two of these, Ollama and LlamaCPP, are local providers: the model runs on the reviewer’s own machine rather than a remote service, which means no API key is required and no data leaves the machine at all, at some cost in the scale of model available compared to a hosted frontier model. Configuration for any provider is reached from the top menu bar through AI → AI Settings, later renamed in some builds simply Settings, one tab per provider, each holding an API key, an optional custom endpoint URL, a model identifier, and a Test Connection button that makes one real, minimal call before anything else is allowed to depend on that provider.

    Whichever provider is marked active under Select Active Provider is the one every AI-assisted operation in the application uses, until changed again. Nothing about which provider is active changes what any operation is permitted to do; every constraint described in the rest of this chapter applies identically regardless of which of the nine sits behind the interface.

    Where a Credential Actually Lives

    An API key typed into the AI Configuration dialog is never written to disk in plain text. It is encrypted at rest using Fernet, a symmetric encryption scheme built on AES, with the encryption key itself derived from a per-installation secret generated the first time CaatMaster runs, the same secret-key mechanism described in Chapter 3’s discussion of how the application’s own credential database is protected. This is not a separate, newly added safeguard; it is the same discipline applied consistently to every category of secret the application holds, whether that secret authenticates a user or authorizes a call to a third-party AI provider.

    What Actually Gets Logged

    Every real call to a language model, regardless of which of the nine providers handles it or which feature triggered it, is appended to an audit log on disk, one JSON record per call: the full prompt sent, the provider and model that answered, the complete response text, token usage, and a timestamp, whether the call succeeded or failed. This log exists because a tool whose entire premise is auditability cannot itself be a black box; what an AI feature actually saw and actually said back has to be reviewable after the fact by someone other than the person who ran it, not merely trusted. AI → AI Activity Log... opens this log directly inside the application, and AI Usage Statistics, reached from the same menu, summarizes token consumption and estimated cost across providers over a chosen period.

    The Translate-Then-Compute Pattern, Tested

    Chapter 4 described the general shape of this pattern: a language model translates unstructured input into a structured, checkable statement, and that statement is then evaluated against the complete dataset in ordinary code. What Chapter 4 did not cover is that this pattern, in CaatMaster, was refined against the failure modes of a real model rather than designed once from first principles and left alone. The rule-translation prompt behind Chapter 14’s deterministic libraries and the next chapter’s Policy Check tab carries two specific corrections, each added after a real large language model produced a specific, wrong answer during testing.

    The first failure was truncation: a compound rule, such as “payments over one thousand dollars must have an approver on file,” genuinely contains two separate testable criteria, an amount threshold and a missing-approver check, but an early version of the translation prompt reliably captured only the first and dropped the second, since nothing in the prompt specifically instructed the model to look for more than one criterion per rule. The second failure was fabrication: a rule that is fundamentally about comparing one row to every other row, such as “no transaction should be recorded twice,” cannot be expressed as a single row’s own filter condition at all, and rather than recognizing this, the model invented an arbitrary, specific-looking condition instead of reporting the rule as not computable. Both failures are now named directly in the prompt itself, with the exact reasoning a reviewer would use to catch them, and duplicate-style rules are routed to a dedicated, genuinely row-comparing check, computed through Polars’ own duplicate-detection logic rather than left for the model to approximate.

    A standing instruction, not a suggestion

    The rule-translation prompt states plainly: an honest “not computable” is always better than a fabricated condition. This is not a stylistic preference. A wrong but plausible-looking filter condition produces a wrong count that looks exactly like a right one, while a rule correctly marked not computable is visibly incomplete and prompts a human to look at it, which is precisely the difference this book has treated as central since Chapter 1.

    Batching, and What Happens With No Provider at All

    A column-level AI operation, such as generating a plain-language explanation for every value in a column, does not make one language model call per row. Rows are grouped into batches, twenty-five at a time by default, and each batch is sent as a single call asking for one structured result per row in the batch, which keeps a thousand-row column to roughly forty calls rather than a thousand. Where a specific batch fails, whether from a malformed response or a provider error, that batch’s rows fall back to a placeholder value rather than aborting the entire column; every other batch that succeeded keeps its real result. Where no AI provider is configured at all, CaatMaster does not attempt a call and silently return an empty-looking result: every batching operation checks for a configured provider first and returns the same fallback value for every row immediately, so a reviewer who has not set up a provider sees an unmistakably incomplete result rather than something that could pass for real output.

    Interpreting the Result

    This chapter has described the machinery every AI-assisted feature in the rest of this book depends on, rather than produced a finding of its own. The discipline worth carrying forward is narrower and more durable than any one feature: before treating a number that came out of an AI-assisted step as evidence, confirm it followed the path this chapter describes, translated into a structured statement, computed in Python against the complete population, and logged. A number that took a shortcut around that path deserves the scrutiny a rough estimate deserves, not the confidence a computed figure earns.

    Chapter 24

    AI-Assisted Text and Document Analysis

    Some of the most useful applications of a language model inside an audit tool have nothing to do with arithmetic at all: reading a free-text description and classifying it, drafting a plain-language explanation of what a column of codes actually represents, or reading a written policy and turning it into something a computer can test. This chapter covers the AI-assisted operations built for exactly this kind of task, every one of them reached from the top menu bar’s AI menu as well as by right-clicking any column header and choosing AI, and the Policy Check tab that extends the same translate-then-compute discipline from Chapter 23 to a policy written in the reviewer’s own words rather than pulled from a pre-built library.

    Column-Level AI Operations

    Six operations share the AI category: AI Explain drafts a plain-language interpretation of each value in a column, one or two sentences depending on the style chosen. Sentiment Analysis scores free text on a positive-to-negative scale. Extract Entities pulls a specific kind of value, an email address, a phone number, a date, or a monetary amount, out of unstructured text. AI Text Classification sorts free text into a fixed list of categories the reviewer supplies. AI Summarize condenses a longer piece of text to a target length. AI Enrich adds a specific kind of derived information, an inferred industry, sentiment, category, or entity, depending on which enrichment type is selected. Every one of these produces a new column, never modifies the source data, and, per Chapter 23, runs in batches of twenty-five rows per call rather than one call per row.

  • Right-click any column header in the AP Transactions dataset and choose AI → Text Classify.
  • Set Text Column to description.
  • Set Categories to a comma-separated list: Office Supplies, Professional Services, Facilities, Technology, Travel.
  • Leave Category Column and Confidence Column at their defaults.
  • Click OK.

    • Run against a real provider, this produces one predicted category and one confidence score per transaction description, batched twenty-five rows to a call as described in Chapter 23. A category assignment is a classification, not a computation the way a ratio or an outlier flag is; it belongs in an audit workpaper as a starting point for grouping and sampling, not as a substantive finding on its own, and a low-confidence assignment is worth a manual glance before being relied on for anything.

    Policy Check: Translating a Written Policy on the Spot

    Chapter 14 covered three pre-built rule libraries, each shipped with its checkable condition already written by hand against logical field names. Policy Check, the first tab of the Compliance Report Generator, reached from the top menu bar through Reports → LLM Analysis..., exists for the much more common case: a policy that has not been pre-encoded into a library at all, typed or pasted directly from the reviewer’s own compliance documentation.

  • From the top menu bar, choose Reports → LLM Analysis... against the AP Transactions dataset, and open the Policy Check tab.
  • Type or paste the policy: All payments of $300 or more must have an approver recorded before disbursement.
  • Click Run Compliance Check.

    • Behind this button sits exactly the translate-then-compute pattern described in Chapter 23: the language model reads the policy text and returns a structured condition, amount greater than or equal to three hundred, approver is null, combined with AND, and that condition is then evaluated against the complete dataset in Python, the same way Chapter 14’s pre-built rule evaluates it, and the same way it would flag the same five records this book has now traced through three separate chapters. The difference between this tab and Chapter 14’s rule libraries is not the computation, which is identical; it is that a rule library’s condition was written once by a person and reused indefinitely at zero AI cost, while Policy Check translates a policy fresh every time it runs, which is the right tradeoff for a policy that genuinely is being seen for the first time, and the wrong one for a policy tested every reporting period, where encoding it once as a reusable library rule, as Chapter 14 describes, is both cheaper and faster.

    Interpreting the Result

    When an AI-drafted classification or translated condition looks wrong

    1. Benign explanation. A text classification genuinely near a category boundary, such as a purchase that is plausibly either Office Supplies or Facilities, can receive a low-confidence or borderline label without any defect in the classifier; free text is often genuinely ambiguous.
    2. Error or judgment lapse. A translated policy condition that omits part of a compound requirement, the exact truncation failure described in Chapter 23, is a translation error the reviewer can catch immediately by reading the structured condition the tool shows before it runs, which is exactly why that condition is always shown rather than hidden behind the final count.
    3. What would indicate something more serious. A classification or translated condition that is wrong in the same direction repeatedly, always under-flagging a specific vendor or category rather than erring randomly, warrants checking whether the input text itself, not the AI step, is the actual source of the pattern.

    Chapter 25

    Numeric Disclosure Reconciliation

    A note to the financial statements routinely states a policy figure in prose: a depreciation rate, a useful life, a loss given default assumption. Confirming that figure actually matches what the underlying records show has traditionally meant a reviewer reading the note by eye and separately querying the data by hand. Numeric Disclosure Reconciliation automates the reading, using AI strictly to find and transcribe each figure exactly as written, and leaves the comparison itself, along with the verdict on whether it matches, to ordinary Python arithmetic against a real dataset column the reviewer maps in.

    Extraction Finds a Figure; It Never Judges One

    The extraction step, reached from the top menu bar through Reports → Numeric Disclosure Reconciliation..., is deliberately narrow. Given a block of narrative text, pasted directly or loaded from a PDF, it returns a list of figures, each carrying a short label, the value exactly as written, a unit, and the verbatim sentence the figure came from. It is not asked whether a figure is correct, is not asked to resolve a stated range such as “three to five years” to a single number, and is not asked to convert units; a range is extracted as a range and left for the reviewer to judge, since resolving it to one number would be the model quietly putting words in the disclosure’s mouth.

    Suppose a note to Meridian Office Supply Co.’s financial statements states: “The Group estimates expected credit losses using a loss given default assumption of 45% across the retail loan portfolio.” Extraction returns a single figure: label “Loss Given Default assumption,” value text “45%,” unit percent, with that exact sentence preserved as the context snippet. Nothing about this step touches loan_portfolio.csv, the working file from Chapter 16, at all; it only reads the sentence.

    Reconciliation Is Arithmetic, Not Another AI Call

    Once a figure has been extracted, the reviewer maps it to a real dataset and column, and the comparison that follows never involves a language model again. CaatMaster computes the real mean, minimum, maximum, and distinct-value count of the mapped column, converts the disclosed figure to the same decimal scale where the unit is a percentage, and flags a mismatch only where the deviation clears two thresholds together: an absolute difference, 0.005 by default, half a percentage point for a rate, and a relative difference, ten percent by default, of the actual value. Both thresholds have to be cleared before a flag is raised, which keeps an immaterial rounding difference on a small-magnitude figure from being flagged purely because the relative percentage looks large.

  • Paste the disclosure text, or click Extract Figures after loading a PDF.
  • For each extracted figure’s row, set Dataset to loan_portfolio and Column to lgd.
  • Leave the tolerances at their defaults, half a percentage point absolute and ten percent relative.
  • Click Reconcile Against Real Data.

    • The first figure, forty-five percent against a real portfolio mean of forty-three percent, deviates by two-tenths of a percentage point in absolute terms and 4.7 percent in relative terms, clearing neither threshold, and reconciles cleanly. A second, hypothetical version of the same disclosure, thirty percent against the same forty-three percent actual mean, deviates by thirteen full percentage points, 30.2 percent in relative terms, and is flagged. Both results are exact, reproducible arithmetic against loan_portfolio.csv’s real values; the only thing that changed between them is which sentence a person, not the model, decided to disclose.

    A scenario worth recognizing

    Suppose a reviewer reconciles a full set of notes to the financial statements ahead of year end and finds a single flagged item: a stated depreciation rate of ten percent for office equipment, against a real portfolio mean, computed from the fixed asset register, of six and a half percent. Rather than treating this as a single wrong sentence, the reviewer maps the same disclosed rate against the register filtered to equipment purchased in the current year alone, and finds the current year’s own mean rate sits at 9.8 percent, close to the disclosed figure. The note’s stated rate turns out to describe the rate applied to new purchases going forward, not a blended rate across the entire existing asset base, which the original, unfiltered mapping could not distinguish. The flag was correct exactly as computed; what it needed was a second, more specific mapping to reveal that the disclosure and the data were both right, describing two different populations.

    Interpreting the Result

    When a disclosed figure does not reconcile

    1. Benign explanation. A disclosed rate can genuinely describe a subset of the population, such as new additions rather than the full asset base, that a first, unfiltered mapping does not isolate, as in the scenario above.
    2. Error or judgment lapse. A note carried forward unchanged from a prior period after the underlying policy or portfolio composition changed is a drafting oversight, not a deliberate misstatement, and is corrected by updating the note to match the current, real figure.
    3. What would indicate something more serious. A disclosed figure that consistently understates a risk-relevant rate, such as a loss given default or an impairment rate, relative to what every reasonable mapping of the underlying data shows, across more than one reporting period, warrants direct inquiry into how that specific note is drafted and reviewed.

    Chapter 26

    Conversational Analysis

    The AI Assistant panel, docked to the right side of the main window and reached from the sidebar or the lightning-bolt icon in its own header, is the most open-ended AI-assisted feature in CaatMaster: a running conversation about whichever dataset is currently open, capable of answering a question directly, running a real query to answer one it cannot answer from memory, proposing a chart, or proposing a transformation step. What keeps this openness from becoming a liability is a narrow, strictly enforced boundary described in this chapter’s second half: the panel can decide what ought to happen, but it never makes anything happen by itself.

    A Conversation Grounded in Real Summary Statistics

    Every question sent to the panel carries context ahead of it: a schema summary of the active dataset and a set of real, precomputed data-quality statistics, row and column counts, null percentages, distinct-value counts, generated the same way Chapter 5’s Profile Dataset command generates its own summary, not asked of the model. A question the model can answer directly from that context, such as how many columns a dataset has or which column carries the most missing values, is answered immediately, from real numbers already in hand.

  • With the AP Transactions dataset open, click the AI Assistant icon in the sidebar.
  • Type a question, for example: How many payments in this dataset have no approver on file?
  • Press Enter.

    • When the Context Alone Is Not Enough

    A question the precomputed context cannot answer, one that requires filtering, grouping, or joining the real data in a way no summary statistic captures, triggers a second step. The model does not guess; it returns a decision, structured as one of six types: answer directly, run a specific SQL query, apply a specific transformation operation, build a specific chart, create a new dataset from a query, or ask for help on a topic. Where the decision is a query or an operation, CaatMaster validates it for safety before anything runs, the same validation any other query or operation in the application passes through, and only a query or operation that passes is actually executed, against the real, complete data, with the real result then handed back to the model for a second, grounded response. A query or operation that fails validation is never silently retried or forced through; the model is told plainly that its request could not be run and asked to answer from the context already available instead, stating openly that a precise answer is not available if the context does not cover the question.

    This two-step shape, decide first, then execute deterministically, then answer from the real result, is the same translate-then-compute discipline from Chapter 23 applied to a conversational interface rather than a single-purpose dialog. The panel is never the thing that runs a query, applies a step, or draws a chart; main_window.py is, and only after the panel’s proposal has passed the same checks every other action in the application passes through.

    Interpreting the Result

    A response from the AI Assistant panel deserves the same question this entire part of the book has returned to repeatedly: did this number take the grounded path, structured, computed, and logged, or did it arrive as a plausible-sounding guess. A response that cites a specific count or amount, especially one attributable to a visible query the panel ran, carries the same weight as any other computed figure in this book. A response phrased in general terms, without a specific number behind it, should be read as exactly that, a starting point for the reviewer’s own next question, not a finding to cite on its own.

    Part VII

    Results

    Chapter 27

    Visualizing Findings

    A table of flagged rows answers a precise question well and a general one poorly. Whether a population’s exceptions concentrate in a handful of vendors, or a metric has drifted outside its normal range over time, is usually easier to see in a chart than to infer from a column of numbers, and CaatMaster’s Visualizations view offers fourteen chart types for exactly this purpose, reached from the top menu bar through Statistics → Visualize Dataset..., or by right-clicking any column header and choosing Visualize.

    Most of the fourteen, column and bar charts, line charts, scatter plots, histograms, pie charts, box plots, heatmaps, area charts, violin plots, stacked column charts, and Q-Q plots, are general-purpose statistical graphics common to any data analysis tool. Two are worth a closer look because they are built specifically for audit work: the Pareto chart and the control chart.

    The Pareto Chart: Finding the Vital Few

    A Pareto chart sorts categories in descending order by total value and overlays a cumulative-percentage line, with a reference line at eighty percent, making it the standard tool for the vital-few observation that a small number of categories, vendors, error types, or accounts, typically accounts for the great majority of total value or exceptions in a population.

  • From the top menu bar, choose Statistics → Visualize Dataset... against the AP Transactions dataset.
  • Set Chart Type to Pareto Chart.
  • Set X Axis to vendor and Y Axis to amount.
  • Click Create Chart.

    • The Control Chart: Watching a Metric Over Its Own History

    A control chart, adapted from statistical process control, plots a metric in sequence against its own mean and a pair of three-standard-deviation control limits, flagging any point that falls outside them. This is a different lens from Chapter 15’s CUSUM technique: a control chart flags an individual point that is extreme relative to the whole population’s spread, evaluated independently at each point, while CUSUM accumulates smaller, sustained deviations over several consecutive points and can catch a shift too gradual for any single point to cross a three-sigma line on its own. The two techniques answer different questions and are not substitutes for one another.

  • Set Chart Type to Control Chart.
  • Set Value Column to amount, leaving X Axis blank so points plot in row sequence.
  • Click Create Chart.

    • Charts Stay Connected to the Pipeline

    A chart built from a dataset is not a static snapshot. Because every view in CaatMaster reads from the same Applied Steps pipeline described in Chapter 2, a chart built against a dataset updates automatically if an upstream step in that dataset’s pipeline is later modified, added, or removed. A Pareto chart built before an outlier flag is added, then revisited afterward, reflects the current state of the data, not the state at the moment the chart was first drawn.

    Interpreting the Result

    A chart is a way of seeing a population, not a finding in its own right. The same three-question discipline from Chapter 1 applies to whatever a chart makes visible: a Pareto chart’s dominant vendor deserves the same benign-explanation-first reading as any other concentration finding, covered at length in Chapter 7, and a control chart’s out-of-control point deserves the same reading as the outlier techniques covered in Chapter 10. What a chart adds is not a new category of evidence, but a faster route to noticing where the existing evidence concentrates.

    Chapter 28

    Building the Audit Report

    Every finding in this book, up to this point, has lived inside CaatMaster’s own views. A workpaper eventually has to leave the application as a document someone else can read without it open in front of them. The Reports view, reached from the top menu bar through Reports → Generate Audit Report..., assembles a self-contained HTML report from named sections, each pulling its content directly from the real, current state of a dataset, never from a value typed in by hand.

    Five Kinds of Section

    A report is a title, an author, and an ordered list of sections, each one of five types. A text section holds prose the reviewer writes directly, an executive summary or a narrative introduction. A summary section is generated automatically: row and column counts, memory size, total missing values, and a per-column breakdown of data type, null count, and distinct-value count, computed fresh from the dataset at the moment the report is built, the same figures Chapter 5’s Profile Dataset command reports. A chart section embeds a real chart, rendered from eight of the fourteen types covered in Chapter 27, bar, line, scatter, histogram, pie, box, heatmap, and area, as a genuine image, encoded directly into the report’s HTML rather than linked externally, so the report remains a single, self-contained file. A table section embeds a slice of the dataset itself. A transformation steps section lists the Applied Steps pipeline that produced the dataset, numbered in order, the same record described in Chapter 2, giving a reader of the report a visible trail back to how every figure in it was actually produced.

    MetricValue
    Total Rows34
    Total Columns10
    Missing Values5

    Figure 28.1 — The real Population Overview section generated for ap_transactions.csv, matching Chapters 5 and 6 exactly.

    Exporting the Result

    Once assembled, a report exports through Reports → Export as a Word document, an Excel workbook, or a PDF, each conversion preserving the section structure built in the Reports view. A report built this way can be regenerated at the start of the next reporting period against a refreshed extract, exactly as Chapter 2 described for the Applied Steps pipeline underlying it, since the report itself contains no figures that were not pulled fresh from the dataset at build time.

    Interpreting the Result

    A report assembled this way carries the same guarantee every other output in this book carries: every number in it traces back to the Applied Steps pipeline the transformation steps section makes visible. A reviewer reading someone else’s report and wanting to confirm a figure does not have to take the author’s word for it; the same dataset, replayed through the same listed steps, reproduces the same report.

    Chapter 29

    Reusable Audit Programs

    An engagement team rarely runs a procedure exactly once. The same segregation of duties scan, the same three-way match, the same Benford’s Law test against a general ledger extract, recurs every reporting period against a freshly extracted population. An Audit Program captures a dataset’s current Applied Steps pipeline, described throughout this book since Chapter 2, as a named, reusable template that can be applied to any other dataset later, reached from the sidebar under Analyze as Audit Programs.

    Saving and Applying a Program

    A program is saved directly from a dataset already carrying the steps worth reusing: build the pipeline once, by hand, exactly as every technique chapter in this book has shown, then save it as a program rather than discarding it once the immediate review is done.

  • With a dataset carrying the Applied Steps to reuse, open Audit Programs from the sidebar.
  • Click Save Current Steps As New Program..., and give it a name and a description.
  • To reuse it later, open Audit Programs against a new dataset, select the saved program from the list, and click Apply to Current Dataset.

    • Applying a program reruns each of its steps against the new dataset in order, exactly as if they had been built by hand again, which means a program built against one dataset’s column names generally needs those steps reviewed, and any column reference corrected, before it produces a meaningful result against a dataset whose columns are named differently. The shipped three-way match program is explicit about this in its own description, instructing the reviewer to repoint each step’s dataset and column references to the actual PO, GRN, and invoice datasets at hand before running it, rather than assuming any two companies’ procurement extracts share identical column names.

    Interpreting the Result

    An Audit Program is a labor-saving device, not a substitute for understanding what its steps do. A finding produced by a saved program deserves exactly the same interpretation discipline as the same finding built by hand, benign explanation first, then error, then the pattern that would indicate something more serious, covered at length in each technique’s own chapter. What a program changes is how quickly the steps that produce the finding can be reassembled, not what the finding itself means once produced.

    Chapter 30

    Managing Projects and Sessions

    Every technique in this book has operated on one dataset at a time, opened inside a project, the container introduced in Chapter 2 that holds every dataset, transformation, and saved analysis belonging to one engagement. This closing chapter of Part VII covers the project itself: how it is saved, exported for sharing outside CaatMaster, and brought back in again with nothing lost.

    What a Project Actually Holds

    A project carries a name, an optional client name and engagement type, a set of named parameters, covered briefly in Chapter 2, that a step can reference instead of a hardcoded value, and a dictionary of datasets, each one an original dataframe together with its Applied Steps pipeline. Saving a project through File → Save Project persists all of this in one file; nothing about a dataset’s transformation history is lost between sessions, since the pipeline itself, not just its current output, is what gets saved.

    Exporting a Project Outside CaatMaster

    Export for Review, covered briefly in Chapter 2 and reached from the sidebar under Lineage & Export, packages a project for a second reviewer who may not have CaatMaster open at all. Three formats are available: Excel workbooks with embedded metadata, one file per dataset; Parquet, a compact columnar format that preserves every data type exactly; or JSON. Exported this way, a two-dataset project built from ap_transactions.csv and quarterly_financials.csv, thirty-eight rows combined, produces a single zip archive under seven kilobytes, holding one Parquet file and one metadata JSON file per dataset alongside a project-level manifest.

    Importing that same archive back into CaatMaster reconstructs the project exactly: both datasets return with their original row counts, thirty-four and four, and their names intact, a real round trip rather than a one-way export. This is not a coincidental convenience; a project export that could not be reliably reimported would defeat the purpose of using it to hand work to a second reviewer, who needs to open the same project CaatMaster itself would recognize, not merely inspect a static copy of the numbers.

    Where a Session Picks Back Up

    The Dashboard view, the first thing a reopened project shows, summarizes recent activity across every dataset in the project: how many datasets are open, their combined row counts, and a running feed of recent actions. It is a starting point for orienting a reviewer returning to a project after time away, not an analytical view in its own right; every technique described earlier in this book is reached from the Transform view or one of the dialogs this book has walked through, not from the Dashboard itself.

    Interpreting the Result

    This chapter, like Chapter 2 before it, describes structure rather than produces a finding. What is worth carrying forward from it is the same question that opened this book: can the number in front of the reviewer be traced back to the file it came from. A project saved, exported, and reimported the way this chapter describes answers that question the same way a single dataset's Applied Steps pipeline does, at the scale of an entire engagement rather than one table.

    Part VIII

    Judgment

    Chapter 31

    Every Flag Is a Question

    Thirty chapters of technique have each closed with the same three questions: what benign explanation would produce this pattern, what error or lapse in judgment would produce it, and what would have to be true for it to reflect something deliberate. That repetition was not an editorial habit. It was the whole point of this book, stated once in Chapter 1 and then rehearsed, deliberately, against every kind of finding a modern audit encounters, a statistical outlier, a control weakness, an accounting estimate, a language model’s own output, so that the discipline survives past the chapter that first taught it. This closing chapter of technique does not introduce a new test. It asks what the thirty before it add up to.

    A Flag Is Evidence of a Pattern, Not of a Cause

    Every technique in this book, from Benford’s Law in Chapter 8 to the reverse-DCF impairment solve in Chapter 18, computes something true about a population and stops there. A deviation, a variance, an implied growth rate, an out-of-control point, is a fact about the data, arrived at deterministically and reproducibly, exactly as Chapter 4 promised. None of these facts carries its own explanation. The explanation is supplied afterward, by a person who knows things the data alone cannot state: what this vendor relationship actually involves, why this estimate changed, whether this employee’s access really was reviewed before the system says it was removed. A tool that computed causes as confidently as it computes deviations would be claiming knowledge it does not have, which is precisely the discipline Chapter 4 asked of CaatMaster’s own AI-assisted features and which this chapter now asks of the reviewer using any of its deterministic ones.

    What Convergence Actually Looks Like

    This book has followed one small working dataset, ap_transactions.csv, through eleven different chapters, and two of its thirty-four rows surfaced repeatedly, for two genuinely different reasons that are worth telling apart rather than blurring together.

    The first is a matter of simple completeness. Five invoices carry no approver on file. Chapter 6’s no-nulls check found them by testing one column for missing values. Chapter 14’s Payment Without Approval on File rule found the identical five records, by name, with a citation and a severity, translating the same underlying fact into compliance language. Two techniques, built for different purposes and reached from different menus, landed on exactly the same five rows because both were, underneath their different vocabulary, asking the same question of the same data.

    The second is a matter of magnitude, and it involves two different invoices from the same vendor, not one invoice found repeatedly. Cascade IT Solutions’ $48,750.00 server rack invoice was flagged as a statistical outlier in Chapter 10, selected with certainty under monetary unit sampling in Chapter 11 for the same reason, sheer size, that made it an outlier, and stood out as the single out-of-control point on a control chart in Chapter 27, three independent statistical mechanisms converging on one transaction because each one, in its own way, measures distance from the ordinary. A separate invoice from the same vendor, $9,900.00, drew a milder outlier flag in Chapter 10 and, independently, a named rule in Chapter 14 for sitting just under a common ten-thousand-dollar approval threshold, a different kind of signal, positional rather than purely statistical, that happened to involve the same vendor without being the same finding.

    Genuine convergence, several independent techniques landing on the same fact through different mechanisms, is a stronger basis for inquiry than any one technique alone, and is worth recognizing precisely because it is different from noticing the same vendor’s name twice. A reviewer who treated every appearance of Cascade IT Solutions across this book as one escalating case, rather than two separate, specific findings, would be manufacturing a pattern the data does not actually support.

    The Discipline Does Not Change for an AI-Assisted Finding

    Part VI drew a hard line between a number that came from Polars and a number that came from a language model, and the whole architecture of CaatMaster’s AI-assisted features, translate then compute, log every call, batch with an honest fallback, exists to keep that line real rather than nominal. That architecture answers whether a number can be trusted the way any other computed figure can be trusted. It does not answer what the number means, which is the same three-question discipline again, applied without exception to a classification from Chapter 24, a reconciled disclosure from Chapter 25, or an answer from the conversational panel in Chapter 26, exactly as it applies to a Benford deviation or a control chart point. An AI-assisted finding that skipped this discipline because it felt more like a direct answer than a statistical artifact would be the one place in this book where the habit most needs to hold, precisely because it is the easiest place to let it slip.

    The Auditor's Skepticism, Not the Software's

    Professional skepticism is sometimes described as an attitude, a general wariness applied at the start of an engagement and then set aside once the testing begins. This book has tried to show something narrower and more durable: skepticism as a specific, repeatable operation, applied individually to each finding at the moment it appears, in the same three-step order every time. A tool can supply the finding. It cannot supply the skepticism. CaatMaster surfaces a pattern precisely, reproducibly, and without fabricating a number it does not have; everything this book has demonstrated about the software depends on that precision. What the software cannot do, and was never built to do, is decide what a precisely computed pattern means for the specific people and the specific transactions behind it. That decision belongs to the reviewer, every time, and the three questions this book has repeated in chapter after chapter are the discipline for making it well.

    Chapter 32

    Governance, Security, and Limits

    A tool that holds client financial data, authentication credentials, and third-party AI provider keys on the same machine an auditor carries between engagements creates obligations that have nothing to do with which statistical test runs correctly. This closing chapter gathers the security architecture described piecemeal across earlier chapters into one place, for whoever at a firm is responsible for approving CaatMaster’s use, and closes with a direct, unhedged statement of what this software does not do.

    What Is Protected, and How

    Three categories of secret live on a machine running CaatMaster, and all three follow the same pattern: nothing sensitive is ever committed to source control, and nothing sensitive is ever stored in plain text on disk. The application’s own authentication database is created fresh on first run in a per-user data directory, never inside the project’s own folder, specifically so it cannot be accidentally added to a version-controlled repository. The signing secret that database depends on is generated once per installation and stored separately, at file permissions that restrict it to the owning user. Every AI provider API key entered through the AI Configuration dialog covered in Chapter 23 is encrypted at rest with Fernet, an authenticated symmetric scheme, keyed off that same per-installation secret rather than a fixed, shared value baked into the application itself. A firm evaluating CaatMaster for a shared or managed machine should confirm this secret is generated per installation, not copied between machines as part of a deployment image, since copying it would let one machine decrypt another’s stored credentials.

    What Leaves the Machine, and What Does Not

    Two features in this book make an outbound network connection under specific, documented conditions, and neither does so silently. An AI-assisted feature, covered throughout Part VI, sends a request to whichever provider is configured only when that specific feature is invoked, never in the background, and every such call, prompt, response, provider, and timestamp, is written to the audit log described in Chapter 23, reviewable afterward by someone other than whoever ran it. An XBRL or inline XBRL import, covered in Chapter 22, attempts a network fetch only when a filing’s taxonomy cannot be resolved from a locally registered taxonomy package first, and a firm operating on an air-gapped or restricted network can eliminate that outbound attempt entirely by registering the taxonomy packages it needs in advance, exactly as Chapter 22 demonstrated. Every other technique in this book, every IFRS and IAS calculation in Part IV, every classic CAAT in Part II, operates entirely on data already loaded into the application, with no network dependency of any kind.

    What a Firm's Own Policy Still Has to Cover

    CaatMaster protects its own credentials and gives a firm the tools to control its own network exposure, but it does not implement several controls a firm's broader policy still needs to supply. It has no built-in, per-user permission model within a single installation; anyone with access to the machine and its project files has access to whatever those files contain, which makes disk-level encryption and physical device control a firm's responsibility, not the application's. Project files, exported audit programs, and the AI audit log are all held as plain files on the local disk, covered in Chapter 30 and Chapter 29, with no built-in synchronization to a firm's own document management or backup systems; a firm intending to rely on CaatMaster output as part of its permanent audit file needs its own process for getting those files into that system. Nothing in the application logs which specific person, as distinct from which machine, ran a given analysis; a firm operating in a regulatory environment that requires per-user attribution of a working paper needs to supply that attribution through its own file-naming or check-in discipline.

    What This Book Has Not Claimed

    Several limits have been stated plainly at the point they mattered, rather than saved for this chapter, and are worth restating together rather than left scattered. CaatMaster has no PDF financial-statement import; the pypdf library it uses, noted in Chapter 25, reads narrative text for AI-assisted analysis, not structured figures for ratio calculation. Every threshold cited in Part IV, IFRS 16’s fifty basis points, IAS 36’s two percentage points, IAS 37’s thirty percent, IAS 12’s twenty percent, IAS 21’s one percent, is a documented starting point for follow-up audit judgment, not a standard-defined bright line, and several of these chapters said so explicitly rather than let a configurable default be mistaken for a professional requirement. Two split variants, catalogued in Appendix A, exist in the underlying engine with no path to reach them from the interface at all; a set of six trigonometric operations that shared that same fate was removed from the application entirely once no legitimate audit use for them turned up, rather than left in place unreachable. Every operation in the top menu bar’s ML menu Anomaly Detection submenu, covered in Chapter 10, now runs the genuine algorithm its name references; what still distinguishes those quick, single-column entries from the trainable models covered in that same chapter is scope, one column at a time versus several at once, not authenticity.

    None of these is a defect uncovered late. Each was found, verified, and written down in the chapter where it belonged, in keeping with the discipline this book asked of every finding CaatMaster itself produces: state what is actually true, not what would be more convenient to claim.

    Appendix A

    This appendix lists every operation registered in CaatMaster’s transformation engine as of this writing: one hundred forty-four in total, organized into the thirteen categories the application itself uses. For each operation, the table gives its parameters, exactly as the underlying registry defines them, and a one-line statement of what it computes. Where an operation is not reachable from the interface at all, that fact is stated plainly rather than omitted. This appendix is generated directly from the same registry the application reads at runtime, so it reflects what the code actually contains rather than what a manual might claim it contains.

    Standalone Tools Outside the Operation Registry

    The following features are not part of the operation registry described above and do not appear in the right-click menu. Each is reached directly from the sidebar and, with the exception of Financial Import Wizard and Cleaning Wizard, none of them modify the underlying dataset or add a step to the Applied Steps pipeline.

    ToolSidebar SectionWhat It Does
    Profile DatasetAnalyzeRuns the automatic dataset profile described in Chapter 5: row and column counts, duplicate rows, per-column completeness and outliers, a Benford screen, and correlated column pairs. Read-only.
    Verify DataAnalyzeRuns one or more of the six completeness and integrity checks described in Chapter 6 and reports pass, fail, or skipped for each. Read-only.
    Variables SamplingAnalyzeOpens the Classical Variables Sampling dialog described in Chapter 11: sample size planning on one tab, sample result evaluation on the other.
    Audit ProgramsAnalyzeManages saved, reusable sequences of steps that can be reapplied to a new dataset, covered in Chapter 29.
    Join DatasetsCombineCombines two datasets on a matching key, covered in Chapter 2.
    Append DatasetsCombineStacks two datasets with compatible columns into one, covered in Chapter 2.
    Compare DatasetsCombineReports differences between two datasets expected to represent the same population at two points in time.
    Fuzzy Match DatasetsCombineJoins two datasets on an approximate, rather than exact, text match, useful when the same vendor or customer is spelled inconsistently across two sources.
    Import Folder ListingImportImports the file and folder metadata of a directory as a dataset, useful for testing file-retention or access-control policies against what is actually present on a file share.
    Project LineageLineage & ExportVisualizes how every dataset in the current project was derived, including joins, appends, and pivots.
    Export for ReviewLineage & ExportPackages a dataset together with its Applied Steps pipeline for a second reviewer.

    Appendix C

    Default Thresholds Reference

    Nearly every deterministic test in this book, from a statistical outlier fence to an IFRS impairment flag, ships with a configurable default rather than a fixed, hidden constant. Every default in this appendix is quoted directly from the application’s own operation registry or service code, not reconstructed from memory, and every one of them carries the same caveat stated repeatedly throughout Parts II through IV: a default is a documented starting point for follow-up audit judgment, never a standard-defined bright line, and the human sanity check this book has deferred to a qualified auditor throughout belongs here most of all, before any of these defaults are relied upon in a real engagement.

    One entry deserves a direct note rather than a bare number. Chapter 16’s walkthrough of the SICR PD trigger sets the multiplier to 3.00x for that specific worked example; the application’s own default, shown whenever the IFRS 9 Staging dialog first opens, is 2.00x. The chapter says so explicitly at the point it changes the value, and this appendix repeats it here since a threshold reference that silently mismatched its own book would defeat the purpose of compiling one.
